  • Detect anomalies in user behavior or event frequency to spot advanced threats.
  • Enrich alerts with pod and user metadata for deeper forensic analysis.
  • Leverage SIEM platforms to automate threat response workflows.

docs.title: Alert Outputs
docs.text: Falco is designed to output alerts in various formats, enabling integration with monitoring systems like Prometheus, ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), and cloud-native logging platforms. Configuring these outputs requires modifying Falco's configuration file (falco.yaml) to define the desired destinations. Below are examples for each integration.

docs.title: Configuring Falco for Prometheus Integration
docs.text: Falco can send alerts to Prometheus via the remote write protocol. This requires a Prometheus server or Prometheus Operator instance to receive the metrics.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
outputs:
  - type: prometheus
    url: http://prometheus-server:9090/api/v1/write

docs.title: Command to Run Falco
docs.text:
falco --config /path/to/falco.yaml

Notes: - Ensure the Prometheus server is accessible at the specified URL. - Use the Prometheus Operator for Kubernetes environments to manage the Prometheus instance.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
outputs:
  - type: http
    url: http://elasticsearch:9200
    format: json

docs.title: Command to Run Falco
docs.text:
falco --config /path/to/falco.yaml

Notes: - Elasticsearch must be running and accessible at the specified URL. - For advanced parsing, use Logstash to process the JSON logs before indexing them in Elasticsearch.

docs.title: Configuring Falco for Cloud-Native Logging Systems
Fluentd Integration
docs.text: Falco can send logs to a Fluentd instance using the TCP protocol.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
outputs:
  - type: fluentd
    address: tcp://fluentd:24224

docs.title: Command to Run Falco
docs.text:
falco --config /path/to/falco.yaml

Notes: - Fluentd must be running and listening on the specified address. - Use Fluentd's plugins to enrich or route logs further.

docs.title: Loki Integration
docs.text: Falco can push logs directly to Loki via HTTP.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
outputs:
  - type: loki
    url: http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push

docs.title: Command to Run Falco
docs.text:
falco --config /path/to/falco.yaml

Notes: - Loki must be running and accessible at the specified endpoint. - Loki's ingestion endpoint is typically /loki/api/v1/push.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Prometheus: Use the prometheus output type with a remote write URL to send metrics.
  • ELK: Configure the http output with Elasticsearch's endpoint for log storage.
  • Cloud-Native Logging: Use fluentd for TCP-based logging or loki for HTTP-based ingestion.
  • Always validate network connectivity and adjust URLs based on your environment's deployment.

docs.title: Visualizing Alerts
docs.text: Kubernetes Runtime Security with Falco

docs.title: Visualizing Falco Alerts with Monitoring Tools
docs.text: Falco alerts provide critical visibility into runtime security events, but their value is amplified when integrated with centralized monitoring tools. By visualizing alerts in dashboards, teams can prioritize threats, correlate events with infrastructure metrics, and automate response workflows. This section guides you through setting up Falco alerts with popular monitoring tools like Prometheus/Grafana, ELK Stack, and cloud-native observability platforms.

docs.title: Integrating Falco with Prometheus and Grafana
docs.text:
Overview Prometheus collects metrics, while Grafana provides a UI for visualization. Falco can output alerts to Prometheus via the prometheus output plugin, enabling real-time dashboards.

Steps 1. Configure Falco to Output to Prometheus Modify the Falco configuration file (falco.yaml) to include the prometheus output: 

outputs:
  - type: prometheus
    server_url: http://localhost:9090
Ensure Prometheus is running and accessible at the specified URL.

  1. Set Up Prometheus to Scrape Falco Metrics Configure Prometheus to scrape Falco's metrics endpoint (if enabled). Example prometheus.yml: 

    scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'falco'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:8080']

  2. Create a Grafana Dashboard

  3. Add Prometheus as a data source in Grafana.
  4. Use the Falco Prometheus Exporter to query Falco metrics.
  5. Build panels to visualize alert counts, severity distribution, and event timelines.

Example Query To show high-severity alerts: 

count_over_time({alert_severity="high"}[5m])

docs.title: Integrating Falco with ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana)
docs.text:
Overview The ELK Stack is ideal for log-centric analysis. Falco can send alerts to Logstash, which forwards them to Elasticsearch for storage and Kibana for visualization.

Steps 1. Configure Falco to Output to Logstash Update falco.yaml to use the logstash output: 

outputs:
  - type: logstash
    server_url: http://localhost:5044

  1. Set Up Logstash to Forward to Elasticsearch Configure Logstash to receive Falco alerts and send them to Elasticsearch. Example logstash.conf: 

    input {
  beats {
    port => 5044
  }
}
output {
  elasticsearch {
    hosts => ["http://localhost:9200"]
    index => "falco-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}"
  }
}

  2. Visualize in Kibana

  3. Create an index pattern in Kibana (falco-*).
  4. Use the Kibana dashboard template for preconfigured visualizations.
  5. Customize dashboards to filter by alert type, container, or namespace.

Example Kibana Query To find all alerts in the last hour: 

@timestamp > now-1h

docs.title: Cloud-Native Observability Tools (Datadog, New Relic)
docs.text:
Overview Cloud providers often offer managed observability tools. Falco can integrate with these via the datadog or newrelic output plugins.

Steps 1. Configure Falco for Datadog Update falco.yaml: 

outputs:
  - type: datadog
    api_key: YOUR_DATADOG_API_KEY
    host: agent.datadoghq.com

  1. Set Up Datadog Alerts
  2. Use Datadog's Falco integration to auto-import metrics.

  3. Create alerts based on Falco event counts or severity levels.

  4. New Relic Integration Configure Falco to output to New Relic: 

    outputs:
  - type: newrelic
    license_key: YOUR_NEWRELIC_LICENSE_KEY
    Use New Relic's alerting rules to trigger actions on Falco events.

docs.title: Best Practices for Visualization
docs.text:
• Structured Logging: Use Falco's --output json flag to ensure consistent, machine-readable alerts.
  • Retention Policies: Configure Elasticsearch or Prometheus to retain alert data for compliance and forensic analysis.
  • Alert Prioritization: Use Falco rules to categorize alerts (e.g., high, medium) and filter dashboards by severity.
  • Monitoring the Monitoring Stack: Ensure Prometheus, Elasticsearch, or Datadog itself is monitored to avoid blind spots.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Falco can integrate with Prometheus/Grafana, ELK Stack, and cloud-native tools for real-time alert visualization.
  • Use structured logging and tailored dashboards to prioritize security events.
  • Combine Falco alerts with infrastructure metrics for contextual threat analysis.
  • Regularly validate monitoring tool configurations to avoid alert fatigue or missed events.
  • Leverage prebuilt dashboards and templates to accelerate observability setup.

docs.title: Custom Threat Rules
docs.text: Falco is designed to detect security threats by analyzing system calls and runtime events. While its built-in rules cover common attack patterns, custom rules are essential for identifying zero-day exploits, insider threats, or novel behaviors that evade standard detection. This section guides you through crafting advanced Falco rules tailored to these scenarios, leveraging event correlation, system call analysis, and contextual filtering.

docs.title: Understanding Falco Rule Structure
docs.text:
Falco rules are defined in YAML files and consist of four core components: 1. Event: The type of event to monitor (e.g., container.start, process.execute). 2. Condition: A logical expression using fields like container.image or process.name. 3. Output: A human-readable message describing the event. 4. Priority: A numerical value (1–100) to determine rule precedence.

Example: 

- rule: Suspicious Process Execution
  desc: Detects unexpected processes in privileged containers
  condition: container.image contains "privileged" and process.name contains "top"
  output: "Suspicious process 'top' executed in privileged container"
  priority: 80

docs.title: Crafting Rules for Zero-Day Exploits
docs.text:
Zero-day attacks often involve unconventional system calls or behaviors. Use Falco’s syscall field to detect anomalies, such as unexpected memory manipulation or process injection.

Example: Detecting Process Injection 

- rule: Process Injection Attempt
  desc: Identifies potential process injection via ptrace
  condition: syscall.name = "ptrace" and container.image != "gvisor"
  output: "Process injection attempt detected via ptrace in container"
  priority: 90
This rule flags use of the ptrace syscall (common in rootkits) outside of known safe containers like gvisor.

docs.title: Detecting Insider Threats
docs.text:
Insider threats often involve access to sensitive data or unauthorized command-line interactions. Use fields like file.path or user.name to filter for suspicious activity.

Example: Unauthorized File Access 

- rule: Sensitive Data Exfiltration
  desc: Alerts on access to secrets or config files
  condition: file.path contains "/secrets/" or file.path contains "/config/" and user.name != "root"
  output: "User '{user.name}' accessed sensitive file '{file.path}'"
  priority: 75
This rule flags access to sensitive paths by non-root users, which could indicate data exfiltration.

docs.title: Advanced Techniques: Event Correlation and Dynamic Rules
docs.text:
For complex threats, combine multiple events using logical operators. For example, correlate a container startup with subsequent file access: 

- rule: Container + File Access
  condition: (container.start and container.image contains "malicious") and (file.access and file.path contains "/etc/passwd")
  output: "Container with malicious image accessed critical file"
  priority: 95

For dynamic rule loading, use Falco’s API or external tools to inject rules at runtime, enabling adaptive detection based on real-time telemetry.

docs.title: Testing and Validation
docs.text:
Use falco --test to validate rules against predefined test cases. Simulate events with tools like kubectl or socat to ensure rules trigger correctly.

Example: Simulating a Suspicious Process 

kubectl run -it --rm --image=alpine test-shell
Monitor the pod’s activity with Falco to verify rule detection.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Custom Falco rules require precise conditions and prioritization to avoid false positives.
  • Focus on system calls (syscall.name) and contextual fields (file.path, user.name) for advanced threat detection.
  • Correlate events across multiple rule triggers to identify multi-stage attacks.
  • Continuously test and refine rules using Falco’s test framework and real-world scenarios.
  • Leverage dynamic rule loading for adaptive, runtime-specific security policies.

docs.title: Deploying and Validating Custom Security Policies
docs.text: Custom Falco rules are essential for addressing unique security requirements in Kubernetes environments, such as detecting application-specific anomalies or enforcing compliance with internal policies. This section guides you through deploying custom rules in production and validating their effectiveness through testing and monitoring.

docs.title: 1. Writing and Testing Rules Locally
docs.text:
Before deploying, test custom rules in a local environment to ensure they work as intended. Use the falco CLI to simulate events and validate rule behavior.

Example: Detecting suspicious container creation 

# custom-rule.yaml
- rule: SuspiciousContainerCreation
  desc: Detect containers created with root privileges
  condition: container.create and container.user = "root"
  output: "Detected container created with root privileges: %container.name%"
  priority: medium
  tags: [k8s, container]

Testing the rule: 

falco --rule custom-rule.yaml --test

docs.title: 2. Deploying to Kubernetes
docs.text:
Falco can be deployed via the Falco Operator or a standalone DaemonSet. For production, the Operator provides better lifecycle management.

Using the Falco Operator: 1. Apply the custom rule as a ConfigMap: 

kubectl create configmap custom-rules --from-file=rules.yaml -n falco

  1. Update the FalcoConfig custom resource to include the rule: 
    apiVersion: falco.org/v1beta2
kind: FalcoConfig
metadata:
  name: falco-config
  namespace: falco
spec:
  rules:
    - name: SuspiciousContainerCreation
      content: |
        rule SuspiciousContainerCreation
          desc: Detect containers created with root privileges
          condition: container.create and container.user = "root"
          output: "Detected container created with root privileges: %container.name%"
          priority: medium
          tags: [k8s, container]

Using a DaemonSet: If using a standalone deployment, mount the rules file into the Falco container: 

volumeMounts:
  - name: falco-rules
    mountPath: /etc/falco/rules.d
volumes:
  - name: falco-rules
    configMap:
      name: custom-rules

docs.title: 3. Post-Deployment Considerations
docs.text:
• Resource limits: Ensure Falco pods have sufficient CPU/memory to avoid performance bottlenecks.
  • Rule versioning: Use Falco’s rule versioning to track changes and ensure compatibility with your Falco version.
  • Monitoring: Integrate Falco with Prometheus/Grafana or SIEM tools for centralized alerting.

docs.title: 1. Simulation and Penetration Testing
docs.text:
Use tools like kubectl or kubetest to simulate attack vectors and verify rule detection.

Example: Testing root container creation 

kubectl run attacker --image=busybox --restart=Never -it -- sh
# Inside the pod:
docker run --rm -it --user root busybox sh

Check Falco logs for alerts matching your custom rule.

docs.title: 2. Automated Testing with Falco’s Test Framework
docs.text:
Leverage Falco’s built-in testing tools to validate rules programmatically: 

falco --test --rules custom-rule.yaml

docs.title: 3. Production Monitoring and Debugging
docs.text:
• Falco logs: Use kubectl logs <falco-pod> to debug false positives/negatives.
  • Alert tuning: Adjust rule priorities and tags to refine alerting.
  • False positive reduction: Periodically review alerts and refine conditions (e.g., adding container.image filters).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Test rules locally before deployment to avoid unintended behavior.
  • Deploy via Operator or DaemonSet based on your Kubernetes setup and operational needs.
  • Validate through simulation and monitoring to ensure rules align with real-world scenarios.
  • Iterate and refine rules based on feedback from production alerts and false positive analysis.

docs.title: Events: Workflow Triggers
docs.text: Events are actions that trigger workflows, such as code pushes, pull request creations, or scheduled intervals. These events initiate the execution of workflows, determining when specific jobs should run. For example, a push event might trigger a build process, while a pull_request event could initiate testing. Events are defined in the workflow file using keys like on: to specify which actions activate the workflow.

docs.title: Jobs: Units of Work
docs.text:
Jobs are individual units of work within a workflow, consisting of one or more steps that execute in a defined order. Each job is assigned to a runner and is configured using the jobs key in the workflow file. Jobs can include steps like running scripts, building applications, or running tests. A job’s execution environment is specified via the runs-on key, which determines whether it uses a hosted or self-hosted runner. For example: 

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v2

docs.title: Runners: Execution Environments
docs.text: Runners are the machines where jobs execute. GitHub provides hosted runners (managed by GitHub) and self-hosted runners (managed by you). Hosted runners are available for public and private repositories, while self-hosted runners are optional for private repositories (though specific configuration is required) but are necessary for custom environments or when security constraints prevent using hosted runners. Runners are specified using the runs-on key in a job, as shown in the example above.

docs.title: Workflow Syntax
docs.text: GitHub Actions workflows are defined using YAML files in the .github/workflows/ directory. These files describe the structure of the workflow, including triggers, jobs, steps, and environment variables. Understanding the syntax is critical for configuring reliable CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: Triggers and Events
docs.text:
Workflows are triggered by events such as push, pull_request, or custom webhooks. Events are specified under the on key. 

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
- Use events for GitHub-native triggers (e.g., push, pull_request). - For external triggers, use workflow_dispatch with a UI button or repository_dispatch for custom payloads. - Nested keys (e.g., branches, paths) filter which branches or files trigger the workflow.

docs.title: Jobs and Runners
docs.text:
Jobs are units of work that run on a runner (virtual machine or self-hosted). Each job must specify a runner with runs-on. 

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
- runs-on defines the runner type (e.g., ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or a self-hosted runner). - Jobs can have conditions using if to control execution (e.g., if: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}). - Jobs can be parallelized using strategy for matrix builds.

docs.title: Steps and Actions
docs.text:
Steps are individual tasks within a job. They can be built-in actions, custom scripts, or third-party tools. 

steps:
  - name: Install dependencies
    run: npm install
  - name: Run tests
    uses: actions/setup-node@v3
    with:
      node-version: '18'
- run executes shell commands (supports bash, PowerShell, etc.). - uses invokes actions from the GitHub Marketplace or local paths. - Inputs are passed via the with keyword for actions. - Steps can be conditionally skipped using if or continue-on-failure.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables are defined under env and can be scoped to the workflow, job, or step. 

env:
  API_URL: https://api.example.com
  DEBUG: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    env:
      DEBUG: true
    steps:
      - run: echo "DEBUG: ${{ env.DEBUG }}"
- Variables are accessed using ${{ env.VARIABLE }} in scripts. - Secrets (sensitive variables) are stored in the repository settings and referenced via ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}. - Variables can override defaults at different scopes (workflow > job > step).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Workflows are structured using on, jobs, and steps keys.
  • Triggers define when workflows execute, with optional event filters.
  • Jobs run on runners and can include conditional logic.
  • Steps combine built-in actions, scripts, and custom tools.
  • Environment variables and secrets enable dynamic configuration.

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
Steps can run in parallel using the strategy key, which is a job-level configuration. This allows you to define multiple job runs with different parameters.

Example: Parallel Job with Strategy 

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

Note: The strategy key must be placed at the job level, not under steps. Matrix strategies define how a job splits into multiple parallel runs based on specified parameters (e.g., OS, Node.js versions).

docs.title: Conditional Logic for Workflow Control
docs.text:
Use if: conditions to control whether steps or jobs execute based on dynamic criteria. Conditions evaluate expressions that determine workflow flow.

Example: Conditional Step Based on Environment Variable 

steps:
  - name: Run tests if DEBUG is set
    if: ${{ env.DEBUG }}
    run: npm test

Example: Conditional Job Based on Branch 

jobs:
  deploy:
    if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy application
        run: ./deploy.sh

Key Concepts: - Use $ to reference variables, job status, or context values.} - Combine conditions with logical operators (&&, ||, !) for complex rules. - Conditional logic enables workflows to skip steps/jobs, reroute execution, or adapt to runtime inputs.

docs.title: Custom Actions
docs.text: GitHub Actions allows developers to create reusable custom actions using JavaScript (Node.js) or Docker containers. Custom actions encapsulate logic for tasks like code testing, dependency installation, or environment setup, enabling teams to standardize workflows across repositories. This guide explains how to build and package custom actions for both JavaScript and Docker-based implementations.

docs.title: Creating JavaScript Actions
docs.text: JavaScript actions are built using Node.js and follow a standard directory structure. Here's how to create one:

docs.title: 1. Project Setup
docs.text:
Create a new directory for your action and initialize a Node.js project: 

mkdir my-action
cd my-action
npm init -y

Add a action.yml file to define metadata and inputs/outputs: 

name: 'Hello World'
description: 'Prints a greeting message'
inputs:
  name:
    description: 'Name to greet'
    required: true
outputs:
  greeting:
    description: 'Generated greeting'
runs:
  using: 'node16'
  main: 'index.js'

Create an index.js file with the action logic: 

const { context } = require('@actions/core');
const { io } = require('@actions/github');

const name = context.getInput('name');
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;

console.log(greeting);
io.setOutput('greeting', greeting);

docs.title: 2. Packaging
docs.text:
Package the action into a ZIP file for distribution: 

npm install
npx actions:package

This generates a dist directory containing the packaged action.

docs.title: Creating Docker Actions
docs.text: Docker actions run in isolated containers, ideal for complex tasks requiring specific environments.

docs.title: 1. Project Setup
docs.text:
Create a Dockerfile to define the container: 

FROM node:16
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

Create an index.js file with the same logic as the JavaScript example above.

docs.title: 2. Packaging
docs.text:
Build and tag the Docker image: 

docker build -t my-action:latest .
docker save my-action:latest > my-action.tar

Upload the .tar file to a container registry (e.g., Docker Hub) for reuse.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
• JavaScript: Use actions:package to generate a ZIP file.
  • Docker: Export the container as a .tar file or push to a registry.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Use semantic versioning (e.g., v1.0.0) and tag releases in Git: 

git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0

When publishing to the GitHub Marketplace, ensure the action.yml specifies the correct version: 

version: '1.0.0'

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• JavaScript actions leverage Node.js and require an action.yml metadata file.
  • Docker actions use containers, ideal for complex or environment-sensitive tasks.
  • Package actions as ZIP files (JavaScript) or Docker images (Docker) for distribution.
  • Use semantic versioning and Git tags to manage releases and ensure compatibility.

docs.title: Inputs & Outputs
docs.text: GitHub Actions allows custom actions to accept inputs and produce outputs, enabling dynamic data exchange between steps in a workflow. Inputs are defined in the action's metadata and passed via the workflow, while outputs are set during execution and consumed by subsequent steps. This section explains how to define and use inputs/outputs effectively.

docs.title: Defining Inputs in Custom Actions
docs.text:
Inputs are declared in the action's metadata.yml file. Each input has a name, description, and optional default value. Required inputs must be provided by the workflow.

Example: metadata.yml 

inputs:
  version:
    description: 'The software version to build.'
    required: true
  env:
    description: 'Environment for deployment (e.g., staging, production).'
    default: 'staging'

In the action's code (e.g., a Node.js script), inputs are accessed via the inputs object: 

const version = inputs.version;
const environment = inputs.env;
console.log(`Building version ${version} for ${environment}`);

docs.title: Defining Outputs in Custom Actions
docs.text:
Outputs are declared in the metadata.yml file with an id and description. They must be explicitly set during execution using the ::set-output syntax.

Example: metadata.yml 

outputs:
  build_number:
    description: 'Generated build number.'
    required: true

In the action's code, outputs are set like this: 

echo "::set-output name=build_number::42"

docs.title: Consuming Outputs in Workflows
docs.text:
Outputs from an action are accessible in subsequent steps via the steps context. Use needs or direct references to pass values.

Example Workflow: 

jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - id: build
        uses: your-action@v1
        with:
          version: '1.0.0'
      - name: Use build number
        run: |
          echo "Build number: ${{ steps.build.outputs.build_number }}"

In this example, the build step's output is used in the next step to log the build number.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Inputs: Use them for configuration parameters that vary between runs.
  • Outputs: Reserve for data that must be shared between steps (e.g., artifact IDs, version numbers).
  • Validation: Always validate inputs in your action code to avoid runtime errors.
  • Avoid Side Effects: Ensure outputs are deterministic and not dependent on external state.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Inputs allow dynamic configuration of actions via the workflow.
  • Outputs enable passing data between steps, such as build numbers or artifact IDs.
  • Define inputs in metadata.yml and set outputs using ::set-output.
  • Consume outputs in workflows using ${{ steps.step-id.outputs.output-name }}.
  • Prioritize clarity and reliability by validating inputs and ensuring outputs are deterministic.

docs.title: Matrix Builds
docs.text: GitHub Actions matrix builds enable you to run the same job across multiple configurations—such as different operating systems, Node.js versions, or architectures—simultaneously. This parallel execution accelerates testing and validation, ensuring compatibility across diverse environments. By leveraging matrix strategies, you can efficiently test code against all required configurations without duplicating workflows.

docs.title: Configuring Matrix Strategies
docs.text: Matrix builds are defined using the matrix key within a job’s strategy block. Each combination of parameters in the matrix spawns a separate job, which runs in parallel by default.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
jobs:
  test-suite:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [14, 16]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm install && npm test

In this example, four jobs are created: - Ubuntu with Node.js 14 - Ubuntu with Node.js 16 - Windows with Node.js 14 - Windows with Node 16

Each job runs independently, and results are aggregated in the workflow run.

docs.title: Advanced Configuration
docs.text:
You can nest matrix parameters for more complex scenarios. For example, combining OS, Node.js, and database versions: 

strategy:
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    node: [14, 16]
    db: [postgres, mysql]
This creates 12 distinct jobs (2 OS × 2 Node × 2 DB). Use matrix.os, matrix.node, etc., in steps to access current configuration values.

docs.title: 1. Cross-Platform Testing
docs.text:
jobs:
  cross-platform-test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - run: echo "Running tests on ${{ matrix.os }}"
      - run: ./run-tests.sh

docs.title: 2. Architecture-Specific Builds
docs.text:
For ARM64 or x86_64 builds, use self-hosted runners or GitHub’s ARM64 runners: 

strategy:
  matrix:
    architecture: [x86_64, arm64]
    os: [ubuntu-latest]
In steps, detect architecture: 
if [[ "$ARCH" == "arm64" ]]; then
  echo "Building for ARM64"
fi

docs.title: 3. Conditional Matrix Builds
docs.text:
Filter configurations using if conditions: 

strategy:
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    node: [14, 16]
    env: ${{ matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest' ? 'prod' : 'dev' }}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep configurations manageable: Avoid overly complex matrices that exceed GitHub’s parallel job limits.
  • Leverage caching: Use actions/cache to speed up dependency installs across matrix jobs.
  • Monitor resource usage: Parallel jobs consume CI minutes and runner resources; optimize with max-parallel or timeout-minutes.
  • Use needs for dependencies: Ensure jobs depend on earlier stages if required.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Matrix builds enable parallel execution across OS, Node.js, or architecture configurations.
  • Define matrices using the matrix key in the strategy block, with parameters like os, node, or db.
  • Combine matrix strategies with conditions, caching, and self-hosted runners for advanced use cases.
  • Balance complexity and resource usage to maintain efficient CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: Caching Optimization
docs.text: GitHub Actions provides robust mechanisms for caching dependencies and artifacts to accelerate build times and reduce resource consumption. By leveraging caching, you can avoid redundant downloads of packages, minimize I/O operations, and ensure consistent environments across workflows. This section explores advanced caching strategies tailored for CI/CD pipelines, focusing on dependency resolution and artifact reuse.

docs.title: Built-in Caching in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
GitHub Actions includes a built-in caching system for common package managers like npm, pip, and Maven. These caches are automatically managed and optimized for typical workflows. For example:

  • npm: Caches node_modules directory.
  • pip: Caches Python packages installed via pip install.
  • Maven: Caches dependencies from the local repository.

By default, these caches are scoped to the repository and workflow, ensuring that subsequent runs can reuse previously downloaded packages. However, for more granular control or custom use cases, the actions/cache action is recommended.

docs.title: Using the actions/cache Action
docs.text: The actions/cache action allows you to manually manage cache keys, paths, and expiration. This is ideal for scenarios where the built-in caching is insufficient or when you need to cache non-standard artifacts. Here's how to use it:

docs.title: 1. Restore Cache
docs.text:
- name: Restore cached dependencies
  uses: actions/cache@v3
  with:
    path: ./node_modules
    key: ${{ hashFiles('package.json') }}

docs.title: 2. Install Dependencies
docs.text:
- name: Install dependencies
  run: npm install

docs.title: 3. Save Cache
docs.text:
- name: Save cache
  uses: actions/cache@v3
  with:
    path: ./node_modules
    key: $${{ hashFiles('package.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ hashFiles('package.json') }}

This approach ensures that the cache is only saved if the restore step succeeds, avoiding stale data.

docs.title: Best Practices for Cache Management
docs.text:
1. Use Semantic Cache Keys Include variables like GITHUB_REF or GITHUB_SHA in your cache key to differentiate between branches or commits: 

    key: ${{ hashFiles('package.json') }}-${{ GITHUB_REF }}

  2. Limit Cache Size GitHub Actions imposes a 10 GB limit per repository. Prioritize caching large or frequently updated dependencies.

  3. Invalidate Caches Strategically Update cache keys when dependencies change (e.g., after a package.json update) to avoid using outdated data.

  4. Combine with Dependency Lock Files Use package-lock.json or Pipfile.lock to ensure deterministic builds and reduce cache misses.

docs.title: Example: Caching Dependencies in a Node.js Project
docs.text:
name: Build Node.js Project

on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Configure Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - name: Restore cached dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ./node_modules
          key: ${{ hashFiles('package.json') }}-${{ GITHUB_REF }}
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install
      - name: Build project
        run: npm run build

docs.title: Example: Caching Dependencies in a Python Project
docs.text:
name: Build Python Project

on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v3
        with:
          python-version: '3.9'
      - name: Restore cached pip dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ./venv
          key: ${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}-${{ GITHUB_REF }}
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m venv venv
          source venv/bin/activate
          pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m pytest

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Caching reduces redundant downloads and speeds up builds by reusing dependencies.
  • Use actions/cache for granular control over cache keys, paths, and expiration.
  • Semantic cache keys (e.g., including branch names) ensure correct cache reuse.
  • Combine caching with lock files to maintain build consistency and minimize cache misses.
  • Monitor cache size limits and prioritize caching high-impact dependencies.

docs.title: Artifacts Management
docs.text: GitHub Actions and CI/CD Pipelines rely on efficient artifact management to ensure reliable, reproducible deployments. Build artifacts—such as compiled binaries, container images, or package files—must be stored, versioned, and retrieved consistently across pipeline stages. Poor artifact management can lead to deployment failures, version mismatches, or unnecessary resource consumption. This section outlines strategies for storing, versioning, and managing artifacts in CI/CD workflows.

docs.title: Artifact Storage Strategies
docs.text: Artifacts must be stored in a location accessible to all pipeline stages while balancing cost, speed, and security. Common approaches include:

docs.title: 1. GitHub Actions Artifacts
docs.text:
GitHub Actions provides built-in artifact storage for short-term use. Use actions/upload-artifact and actions/download-artifact for lightweight workflows. 

# Upload an artifact
steps:
  - name: Build app
    run: ./build.sh
  - name: Upload artifact
    uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
    with:
      name: my-app
      path: dist/

# Download an artifact in a subsequent job
steps:
  - name: Download artifact
    uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
    with:
      name: my-app
      path: ./dist

docs.title: 2. Cloud Object Storage
docs.text:
For long-term storage, use cloud providers like AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage (GCS), or Azure Blob Storage. Example for AWS S3: 

# Upload to S3
aws s3 cp dist/ s3://my-bucket/artifacts/ --recursive
# Download from S3
aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/artifacts/ dist/ --recursive

docs.title: 3. Local Filesystems
docs.text: For ephemeral environments, store artifacts in shared network drives or NFS mounts. Ensure cleanup to avoid disk bloat.

docs.title: Versioning Best Practices
docs.text: Versioning ensures artifacts are traceable and compatible with deployments. Use semantic versioning (e.g., v1.2.3) and tie versions to Git tags or CI/CD pipeline IDs.

docs.title: 1. Git-Based Versioning
docs.text:
Link artifact versions to Git tags: 

# Example: Tagging a release
git tag v1.2.3
git push origin v1.2.3
Use tags to reference artifacts in workflows: 
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Use v1.2.3 artifact
        run: ./deploy.sh --version v1.2.3

docs.title: 2. Timestamp-Based Versioning
docs.text:
Automate versioning with timestamps or build numbers: 

# Generate a version string
VERSION=$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
echo "Building version $VERSION"

docs.title: Retrieval and Dependency Management
docs.text: Artifacts must be retrievable by downstream stages. Use explicit paths and versioned references to avoid conflicts.

docs.title: 1. Cross-Stage Artifact Sharing
docs.text:
Pass artifacts between jobs in the same workflow: 

jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - name: Build and upload
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: dist/
  deploy:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - name: Download and deploy
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: ./dist

docs.title: 2. Dependency Locking
docs.text: Use lock files (e.g., package-lock.json, Pipfile.lock) to ensure consistent dependencies across builds.

docs.title: Artifact Retention and Cleanup
docs.text: Unused artifacts consume storage and pose security risks. Implement retention policies and automated cleanup.

docs.title: 1. Cloud Storage Retention
docs.text:
Configure S3 lifecycle policies to delete artifacts after a set period: 

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ExpirationInDays": 30,
      "Prefix": "artifacts/",
      "Status": "Enabled"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 2. GitHub Actions Cleanup
docs.text:
Use actions/cleanup-artifacts@v2 to remove unused artifacts: 

jobs:
  cleanup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Clean up old artifacts
        uses: actions/cleanup-artifacts@v2
        with:
          keep: 5  # Retain the 5 most recent artifacts

docs.title: Security and Access Control
docs.text: Secure artifacts with encryption, access controls, and secrets management.

docs.title: 1. Encryption
docs.text: Encrypt artifacts at rest and in transit: - Use AWS KMS for S3 encryption. - Leverage GitHub Actions' built-in encryption for uploaded artifacts.

docs.title: 2. Access Controls
docs.text:
Restrict access to artifacts using IAM roles (for cloud storage) or GitHub Actions' secret management: 

# Example: Use a secret to access a private S3 bucket
env:
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use versioning (Git tags, semantic versions) to ensure reproducibility.
  • Choose storage based on workflow needs: GitHub Actions for short-term, cloud storage for long-term.
  • Automate cleanup to avoid storage bloat and security risks.
  • Secure artifacts with encryption and access controls.
  • Explicitly reference artifacts in workflows to avoid dependency conflicts.

docs.title: Deployment Automation
docs.text: GitHub Actions provides robust capabilities for automating deployment strategies, enabling teams to minimize downtime, reduce risk, and ensure reliability. This section explores two key patterns: blue-green deployments and canary deployments, along with practical implementation guidance using GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Blue-Green Deployment Pattern
docs.text: Blue-green deployment involves maintaining two identical environments (blue and green). Traffic is switched from the active environment (blue) to the new version (green) after validation, ensuring zero-downtime updates.

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Prepare environments: Use cloud providers (e.g., AWS EC2, Kubernetes) or infrastructure-as-code tools to provision identical environments.
  2. Deploy to green: Trigger a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy the new version to the green environment.
  3. Validate: Run automated tests or health checks in the green environment.
  4. Switch traffic: Use a load balancer or routing rule to redirect traffic from blue to green.
  5. Clean up: Decommission the blue environment if the deployment succeeds.

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
name: Blue-Green Deployment
on: push
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build artifact
        run: ./build.sh
      - name: Deploy to green environment
        run: ./deploy-green.sh
      - name: Run tests
        run: ./test-suite.sh
      - name: Switch traffic
        run: ./switch-traffic.sh
      - name: Clean up blue environment
        if: success()
        run: ./cleanup-blue.sh

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• Use environment variables (e.g., BLUE_ENV_URL, GREEN_ENV_URL) to manage environment-specific configurations.
  • Automate traffic switching with tools like AWS Route 53, NGINX, or Kubernetes ingress controllers.

docs.title: Canary Deployment Pattern
docs.text: Canary deployments gradually roll out changes to a subset of users, allowing teams to monitor performance and rollback if issues arise.

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Deploy canary version: Use GitHub Actions to deploy the new version to a canary environment (e.g., a Kubernetes pod or cloud instance).
  2. Route traffic: Direct a small percentage of traffic to the canary environment.
  3. Monitor metrics: Track key performance indicators (e.g., error rates, latency) using observability tools (e.g., Prometheus, Datadog).
  4. Scale or rollback: If metrics are healthy, scale the canary deployment. If not, rollback to the previous version.

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
name: Canary Deployment
on: push
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build artifact
        run: ./build.sh
      - name: Deploy canary
        run: ./deploy-canary.sh
      - name: Route traffic
        run: ./route-traffic.sh --percentage 5
      - name: Monitor metrics
        run: ./monitor-metrics.sh
      - name: Scale canary
        if: success()
        run: ./scale-canary.sh
      - name: Rollback on failure
        if: failure()
        run: ./rollback.sh

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• Use tools like AWS CloudFormation, Kubernetes Helm, or Terraform for environment provisioning.
  • Integrate with observability pipelines to automate rollback decisions based on thresholds.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Blue-green deployments ensure zero-downtime by isolating new versions in a parallel environment.
  • Canary deployments minimize risk by testing changes with a subset of users before full rollout.
  • GitHub Actions workflows can automate environment switching, traffic routing, and rollback logic.
  • Combine with observability tools to enable data-driven decisions during deployment.
  • Prioritize idempotency and cleanup steps to avoid resource leaks in automated pipelines.

docs.title: Security Scanning
docs.text: GitHub Actions provides robust mechanisms to integrate security scanning into CI/CD pipelines, ensuring vulnerabilities, secrets, and code quality issues are detected early. This section covers dependency scanning, secret scanning, and code quality checks, along with practical examples for implementation.

docs.title: Dependency Scanning
docs.text: Dependency scanning identifies vulnerabilities in third-party libraries and packages. GitHub Actions supports tools like Dependabot (built-in) and Snyk, which can be configured to audit dependencies during builds.

docs.title: Example: Dependabot Integration
docs.text:
Dependabot automatically creates pull requests for dependency updates. To enable it: 

# .github/workflows/dependabot.yml
name: Dependabot
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 1 * * *'  # Daily check

jobs:
  dependabot:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Dependabot audit
        uses: dependabot/audit@v2

docs.title: Example: Snyk Dependency Scan
docs.text:
Snyk provides detailed vulnerability reports. Configure it with a token stored as a secret: 

# .github/workflows/snyk.yml
name: Snyk Scan
on:
  push
  pull_request

jobs:
  snyk:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Snyk Scan
        uses: snyk/actions/scan@v1
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.SNYK_TOKEN }}
          packageManager: npm  # or yarn, pip, etc.

Best Practices: - Schedule regular scans (e.g., daily or weekly). - Prioritize critical vulnerabilities in your dependency graph. - Integrate with vulnerability databases like CVE or NVD.

docs.title: Secret Scanning
docs.text: Secret scanning detects hardcoded credentials, API keys, and other sensitive data in code. GitHub provides built-in secret scanning that alerts on suspicious patterns. For advanced use cases, tools like GitGuardian or TruffleHog can be integrated.

docs.title: Example: GitHub Secret Scanning
docs.text: Enable secret scanning in your repository settings (Repository > Security > Secret Scanning). GitHub automatically scans for patterns like API_KEY=... or TOKEN=....

docs.title: Example: GitGuardian Integration
docs.text:
Use GitGuardian’s GitHub Action to scan for secrets: 

# .github/workflows/gitguardian.yml
name: GitGuardian Scan
on:
  push
  pull_request

jobs:
  gitguardian:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: GitGuard, scan
        uses: gitguardian/gg-action@v1
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.GITGUARDIAN_TOKEN }}

Best Practices: - Store secrets in environment variables or encrypted secrets, not hardcoded. - Regularly review secret scanning alerts and disable false positives. - Combine with GitHub’s built-in secret scanning for comprehensive coverage.

docs.title: Code Quality Checks
docs.text: Code quality tools like ESLint, RuboCop, or Pylint enforce coding standards and detect bugs. Integrate these tools into workflows to fail builds on critical issues.

docs.title: Example: ESLint for JavaScript
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/eslint.yml
name: ESLint
on:
  push
  pull_request

jobs:
  eslint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install
      - name: Run ESLint
        run: npx eslint . --max-warnings 0

docs.title: Example: RuboCop for Ruby
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/rubocop.yml
name: RuboCop
on:
  push
  pull_request

jobs:
  rubocop:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: bundle install
      - name: Run RuboCop
        run: bundle exec rubocop --fail-on-cops

Best Practices: - Configure severity levels to fail builds on critical issues. - Automate formatting tools (e.g., Prettier, Black) alongside linters. - Use static analysis tools tailored to your language/stack.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Dependency scanning tools like Dependabot and Snyk help identify vulnerable packages.
  • Secret scanning (built-in or via GitGuardian) prevents accidental exposure of credentials.
  • Code quality checks with ESLint, RuboCop, or Pylint enforce standards and reduce bugs.
  • Combine these scans with CI/CD steps to enforce security and compliance automatically.
  • Regularly update tools and review alerts to stay ahead of emerging threats.

docs.title: Reusable Workflows
docs.text: GitHub Actions enables teams to build complex CI/CD pipelines by leveraging reusable workflows, which allow modular composition of tasks across repositories. Reusable workflows reduce duplication, improve maintainability, and enable consistent processes across projects. This section explains how to design and compose reusable workflows for scalable, maintainable pipelines.

docs.title: Understanding Reusable Workflows
docs.text:
Reusable workflows are defined in .github/workflows/ directories and can be referenced by other workflows using the uses keyword. They encapsulate common tasks (e.g., testing, linting, deployment) into self-contained units, which can be versioned and shared.

Key benefits: - Modularity: Break down monolithic workflows into focused, reusable components. - Consistency: Ensure standardized processes across repositories. - Collaboration: Enable cross-team reuse of workflows without duplicating logic.

Reusable workflows can accept inputs (parameters), produce outputs, and expose secrets for secure data passing.

docs.title: Creating Reusable Workflows
docs.text: To create a reusable workflow, define it in a separate YAML file (e.g., test-workflow.yml) and reference it in other workflows.

docs.title: Example: Reusable Testing Workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/test-workflow.yml
name: Run Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

docs.title: Example: Referencing the Reusable Workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/main-workflow.yml
name: Main Pipeline
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run tests
        uses: .github/workflows/test-workflow.yml@main

docs.title: Composing Workflows with Reusability
docs.text: Reusable workflows can be combined with other workflows or nested within jobs. Use jobs to orchestrate multiple reusable components.

docs.title: Example: Multi-Stage Pipeline with Reusables
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/full-pipeline.yml
name: Full CI/CD Pipeline
on: [push]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build project
        run: npm run build
      - uses: .github/workflows/test-workflow.yml@main
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-test
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to staging
        run: ./deploy.sh staging

docs.title: Best Practices for Reusability
docs.text:
1. Parameterize Inputs: Use inputs to make workflows flexible. 
    inputs:
  env: { type: string, default: 'dev' }
  2. Version Control: Tag reusable workflows with semantic versions (e.g., v1.0.0) for dependency management.
  3. Avoid Hardcoding: Use outputs to pass dynamic values between workflows.
  4. Security: Restrict secret exposure by using secrets and avoiding hardcoded credentials.
  5. Namespace Workflows: Organize reusable workflows into dedicated directories (e.g., ./workflows/).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Reusable workflows modularize CI/CD pipelines, reducing duplication and improving maintainability.
  • Use uses to reference reusable workflows and inputs/outputs for dynamic interaction.
  • Version and namespace reusable workflows to ensure consistency across projects.
  • Prioritize security by avoiding hardcoded secrets and leveraging workflow parameters.
  • Combine reusable workflows with jobs to create complex, orchestrated pipelines.

docs.title: Deployment Gates
docs.text:
GitHub Actions and CI/CD Pipelines Workflow Optimization and Best Practices

Controlled, reliable deployments are critical for maintaining system stability and security. Deployment gates and approval workflows act as checkpoints to ensure code changes meet quality, security, and compliance standards before reaching production. These mechanisms prevent untested or unapproved changes from being deployed, enforce team collaboration, and reduce the risk of regressions or security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Implementing Deployment Gates
docs.text:
Deployment gates are automated conditions that must be satisfied before a pipeline proceeds to the next stage. They enforce quality checks, security validations, and infrastructure readiness.

Example: Enforce Test Passes Before Deployment Use conditional logic in workflows to require test suites to pass before deploying: 

name: Deploy to Staging
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: ${{ job.status == 'success' }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to staging
        run: ./deploy.sh
This workflow ensures deployment only occurs if the build job succeeds.

Advanced: Multi-Stage Gates Chain multiple gates for complex environments: 

deploy:
  needs: [build, security-scan]
  if: ${{ job.status == 'success' && env.SECURITY_SCAN_PASSED }}
Use environment variables or secrets to dynamically control gate conditions.

docs.title: Manual Approval Workflows
docs.text:
Manual approvals add human oversight for high-risk operations, such as production deployments or infrastructure changes. GitHub Actions supports this via the needs keyword and pull request (PR) approvals.

Example: Require Approval Before Production Deployment 

name: Production Deployment
on: [push]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Wait for approval
        uses: actions/github-script@v5
        with:
          script: |
            const response = await github.pulls.createReview({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              pull_number: context.payload.pull_request.number,
              body: 'Approved for production deployment',
              event: 'APPROVE'
            });
            console.log(response);
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: ./prod-deploy.sh
This workflow requires a PR to be approved before proceeding.

Best Practice: Contextual Approvals Use GitHub’s pull_request event to trigger approvals only for specific branches (e.g., main): 

on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

docs.title: Branch Protection Rules
docs.text:
Branch protection rules enforce policies for merging changes into protected branches (e.g., main or production). These rules integrate with CI/CD pipelines to ensure only validated code reaches production.

Example: Enforce Status Checks and Pull Request Merges In your repository settings, configure: - Require status checks to pass (e.g., ci/cd workflow). - Require pull request reviews before merging. - Restrict pushes to protected branches.

Integration with Workflows Link branch protection to pipeline stages: 

name: Main Branch Deployment
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: ./prod-deploy.sh
This ensures deployment only occurs when changes are merged into main after passing all checks.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Deployment gates automate quality checks, ensuring only validated code progresses through pipelines.
  • Manual approvals add human oversight for critical operations, reducing accidental or unauthorized deployments.
  • Branch protection rules enforce team collaboration and compliance, preventing unreviewed changes from reaching production.
  • Integrate these mechanisms into CI/CD pipelines to create a robust, auditable release process.

docs.title: ZFS Pools
docs.text: ZFS pools are the foundational structure for organizing and managing storage in a ZFS environment. Creating a pool involves defining datasets, configuring redundancy, and optimizing performance through vdev (virtual device) arrangements. This section covers the essential steps to create and configure ZFS pools, including device selection, RAID configurations, and property tuning for reliability and efficiency.

docs.title: Understanding ZFS Pools and Vdevs
docs.text:
A ZFS pool aggregates physical storage devices (disks, SSDs, etc.) into a logical storage pool. These devices are grouped into vdevs (virtual devices), which can be: - Disks: Single physical devices. - Mirrors: Pairs or groups of disks for redundancy. - RAIDz: Striping with parity (RAID ⅚-like) for fault tolerance.

Key considerations: - Redundancy (mirrors, RAIDz) protects against device failure. - Performance depends on vdev configuration (e.g., mirrored pools offer faster read/write speeds). - Avoid over-provisioning; balance redundancy and capacity.

Example: A mirrored pool with two disks ensures data redundancy while maintaining performance.

docs.title: Creating a ZFS Pool
docs.text: Use the zpool create command to define a pool. Start by identifying available devices (e.g., /dev/sdX, /dev/sdY).

docs.title: Basic Pool Creation
docs.text:
# Single disk pool (no redundancy)  
zpool create mypool /dev/sdX  

# Mirrored pool (redundant)  
zpool create mypool mirror /dev/sdX /dev/sdY  

# RAIDz pool (parity-based redundancy)  
zpool create mypool raidz /dev/sdX /dev/sdY /dev/sdZ

Notes: - Use zpool status to verify the pool’s state after creation. - If the pool was previously created and exported, import it with zpool import.

docs.title: Configuring Pool Properties
docs.text: After creation, fine-tune pool behavior using properties like ashift, compression, and logbias.

docs.title: Common Property Configurations
docs.text:
# Set ashift (alignment) for optimal performance (12 for 4KB sectors)  
zpool set ashift=12 mypool  

# Enable compression (e.g., lz4 for speed)  
zpool set compression=lz4 mypool  

# Optimize for read-heavy workloads (e.g., logbias=throughput)  
zpool set logbias=throughput mypool  

# Set a quota for the pool (e.g., 50% of available space)  
zfs set quota=50G mypool

Advanced tuning: Use zfs set to configure properties like dedup (data deduplication) or reservation (space guarantees).

docs.title: Best Practices for Pool Creation
docs.text:
1. Device Selection: Use SSDs for log devices (e.g., zpool create mypool /dev/sdX log /dev/sdY) to improve write performance.
  2. Redundancy: Prioritize mirrors over RAIDz for simplicity and faster recovery.
  3. Avoid Over-RAIDz: RAIDz pools are more complex and slower to rebuild than mirrored pools.
  4. Monitor Health: Regularly run zpool scrub to check for data integrity issues.
  5. Documentation: Label devices clearly and document pool configurations for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Vdevs (disks, mirrors, RAIDz) define redundancy and performance.
  • Use zpool create with appropriate vdevs for fault tolerance and speed.
  • Configure properties like ashift, compression, and logbias for optimal performance.
  • Prioritize simplicity (mirrors) over complex RAIDz setups unless parity is critical.
  • Regularly monitor and maintain pools with zpool scrub and zpool status.

docs.title: Snapshots: Point-in-Time Protection
docs.text:
ZFS snapshots are read-only, space-efficient copies of datasets. They use copy-on-write (CoW) to share data with the original dataset until modifications occur.

Creating a snapshot: 

zfs snapshot tank/data@snap1
This creates a snapshot named snap1 for the tank/data dataset.

Listing snapshots: 

zfs list -t snapshot
Output includes snapshot names, creation time, and space used.

Destroying a snapshot: 

zfs destroy tank/data@snap1
Use zfs destroy -r to recursively delete nested snapshots.

Pruning old snapshots: To prune old snapshots, use zfs destroy with retention policies or scripts. For example: 

zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap2
zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap3
zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap4
zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap5
zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap6
zfs destroy -r tank/data@snap6a
Automate pruning with retention policies: 
zfs set retention=7d tank/data
This keeps snapshots for 7 days before pruning.

docs.title: Clones: Writable Branches of Snapshots
docs.text:
Clones are writable datasets that fork from a snapshot. They share data with the original snapshot but allow independent modifications.

Creating a clone: 

zfs clone tank/data@snap1 tank/data_clone
This creates a new dataset tank/data_clone based on snap1.

Cloning a snapshot: 

zfs clone -o snapdir=hidden tank/data@snap1 tank/data_clone2
Cloning a snapshot creates a writable clone, which can itself be cloned to enable branching workflows.

Modifying a clone: 

echo "Test data" > /tank/data_clone/testfile
Changes to the clone do not affect the original snapshot.

docs.title: Snapshot and Clone Management
docs.text:
• Retention policies: Use zfs set snapdir=hidden to hide snapshots from zfs list.
  • Space management: Snapshots consume space only when data changes. Use zfs list to monitor usage.
  • Backup with snapshots: Use zfs send and zfs receive to transfer snapshots between pools.

Example: Backing up a snapshot 

zfs send tank/data@snap1 | zfs receive tank/data_backup

docs.title: Troubleshooting Tips
docs.text:
• Snapshot size issues: If a snapshot grows unexpectedly, investigate CoW behavior or data changes.
  • Clone conflicts: Ensure the target dataset name does not already exist when cloning.
  • Snapshot dependencies: Destroy child snapshots before deleting parent snapshots.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Snapshots provide efficient, read-only backups with minimal storage overhead.
  • Clones enable safe, writable branching from snapshots for testing or development.
  • Use zfs snapshot and zfs clone to manage data protection and workflow flexibility.
  • Regularly prune old snapshots and monitor space usage to avoid storage exhaustion.
  • Combine snapshots with zfs send/receive for offsite backups or dataset replication.

docs.title: ZFS Send & Receive
docs.text: ZFS send and receive are foundational tools for data replication, backup, and disaster recovery in ZFS environments. These commands enable efficient transfer of dataset states between systems, leveraging ZFS's snapshot capabilities to minimize data duplication. By combining send (which generates a stream of changes) with receive (which applies that stream to a target dataset), administrators can synchronize data across systems, create point-in-time backups, or recover from catastrophic failures.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
The zfs send command creates a snapshot stream of a dataset, while zfs receive applies that stream to a target dataset. For a full replication:

# Create a snapshot
zfs snapshot tank/data@backup-20231001

# Send the snapshot to a remote system (via SSH or a pipe)
zfs send tank/data@backup-20231001 | ssh user@remote-host "zfs receive tank/data"

For local backups, you can pipe the stream to a file or another system. The -R flag ensures recursive inclusion of all child datasets:

zfs send -R tank/data@backup-20231001 | tar -cvf backup.tar

docs.title: Incremental Sends
docs.text:
Incremental sends transfer only the changes since a specified snapshot, reducing bandwidth and time. Use the -i (incremental) flag with a base snapshot:

# First, send a full snapshot
zfs send tank/data@initial | zfs receive tank/data

# Later, send incremental changes
zfs send -i tank/data@initial tank/data@current | zfs receive tank/data

The target system must have the base snapshot (initial) pre-existing. Incremental sends are ideal for regular backups or real-time replication.

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text:
• Compression: Use -c to compress the send stream, reducing network bandwidth usage: 

    zfs send -c tank/data@backup | ssh user@remote "zfs receive tank/data"

  • Encryption: Secure data in transit with SSH or TLS (e.g., via openssl or scp): 

    zfs send tank/data@backup | gzip | ssh user@remote "gunzip | zfs receive tank/data"

  • Force Receiving: Use -F to overwrite existing data on the target (caution required): 

    zfs receive -F tank/data < snapshot_stream

docs.title: Disaster Recovery Example
docs.text:
In a disaster recovery scenario, send and receive can restore data from a remote backup. Suppose a system fails and needs recovery:

  1. Backup System: Regularly send snapshots to a remote server: 

    zfs send -i tank/data@daily-01 | ssh user@backup-server "zfs receive tank/data"

  2. Recovery System: Restore the latest snapshot: 

    ssh user@backup-server "zfs send tank/data@latest" | zfs receive tank/data

For partial recovery, you can extract specific snapshots from a stream: 

zfs send tank/data@snap1 | zfs receive -n tank/data  # Preview without applying

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• zfs send and receive enable efficient data replication and backup by leveraging ZFS snapshots.
  • Incremental sends (-i) minimize data transfer by tracking changes since a base snapshot.
  • Use compression and encryption to secure data in transit during replication.
  • Always verify target datasets exist and match the source structure before receiving.
  • Combine with SSH or network tools for secure, cross-system disaster recovery workflows.

docs.title: RAIDZ Configurations
docs.text: ZFS RAIDZ configurations provide fault tolerance by distributing data and parity across multiple disks. Unlike traditional RAID levels, RAIDZ in ZFS is more flexible, allowing for dynamic expansion and varying numbers of parity disks. RAIDZ1 uses one parity disk, RAIDZ2 uses two, and RAIDZ3 uses three. These configurations enable the pool to survive disk failures while maintaining data integrity.

docs.title: Setting Up RAIDZ Pools
docs.text:
To create a RAIDZ pool, use the zpool create command with the raidz keyword. Ensure you have at least three disks for RAIDZ1, four for RAID, and so on.

Example: Creating a RAIDZ1 pool 

zpool create myraidz1 raidz /dev/sda /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
This command creates a RAIDZ1 pool with three disks. For RAIDZ2, add four disks: 
zpool create myraidz2 raidz /dev/sda /dev/sdb /dev/sdc /dev/sdd

Note: RAIDZ configurations require at least three disks. Always verify disk availability and ensure proper hardware redundancy before creating pools.

docs.title: Adding or Removing Disks
docs.text:
To expand a RAIDZ pool, use zpool add. For example, adding a disk to a RAIDZ1 pool: 

zpool add myraidz1 raidz /dev/sdd
This converts the pool to RAIDZ2 by adding an extra parity disk.

To remove a disk (not recommended for active pools), use: 

zpool remove myraidz1 /dev/sdd
Warning: Removing disks from RAIDZ pools can disrupt redundancy and should be done with caution.

docs.title: Replacing Failed Disks
docs.text:
If a disk fails, replace it using zpool replace: 

zpool replace myraidz1 /dev/sda /dev/sda1
ZFS will resilver data to the new disk, rebuilding the pool's redundancy. Monitor progress with: 
zpool status myraidz1

docs.title: Checking Pool Health
docs.text:
Use zpool status to inspect the pool's state: 

zpool status myraidz1
Look for ONLINE, OFFLINE, or DEGRADED states. The -v flag provides detailed information: 
zpool status -v myraidz1

docs.title: Resilvering and Errors
docs.text:
If resilvering fails, check logs with: 

zevent -l
Or use zdb for advanced diagnostics: 
zdb -v myraidz1

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• Disk failures: Replace failed disks promptly.
  • Resilvering errors: Verify disk connections and SMART status.
  • Insufficient parity disks: Ensure RAIDZ configurations meet redundancy requirements.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• RAIDZ1, RAIDZ2, and RAIDZ3 provide 1, 2, or 3 parity disks for fault tolerance.
  • Use zpool create with raidz to set up pools, ensuring sufficient disks for redundancy.
  • Expand pools with zpool add and replace failed disks using zpool replace.
  • Monitor health with zpool status and troubleshoot with zdb or zevent.
  • Always prioritize regular backups and hardware reliability for critical data.

docs.title: Btrfs Subvolumes
docs.text: Btrfs Subvolumes are a powerful feature for organizing data and enabling snapshot-based backups. A subvolume acts as a virtual directory within a Btrfs filesystem, allowing independent mounting, snapshots, and permission management. This section covers how to create, manage, and leverage subvolumes for structured storage administration.

docs.title: Creating Subvolumes
docs.text:
To create a new subvolume, use the btrfs subvol create command. Subvolumes are typically created under the root subvolume (which is automatically created when the filesystem is initialized).

Example: 

sudo btrfs subvol create /mnt/btrfs/data_home
This creates a subvolume named data_home under /mnt/btrfs.

Note: Subvolumes must reside within a Btrfs filesystem. Ensure the mount point is correctly specified.

docs.title: Managing Subvolumes
docs.text:
Use the btrfs subvol command to rename, delete, or inspect subvolumes.

Renaming a Subvolume: 

sudo btrfs subvol rename /mnt/btrfs/old_name /mnt/btrfs/new_name

Deleting a Subvolume: 

sudo btrfs subvol delete /mnt/btrfs/deprecated_data
Caution: This permanently removes the subvolume and its contents.

Listing Subvolumes: 

sudo btrfs subvol list /mnt/btrfs
This shows all subvolumes under the specified mount point, including their IDs and paths.

docs.title: Mounting Subvolumes
docs.text:
Subvolumes can be mounted independently using the mount command with the subvol option.

Mounting a Subvolume: 

sudo mount -o subvol=data_home /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs_mount
This mounts the data_home subvolume from /dev/sdb1 to /mnt/btrfs_mount.

For persistent mounts, add an entry to /etc/fstab: 

/dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs_mount btrfs subvol=data_home 0 0

docs.title: Snapshots and Subvolumes
docs.text:
Subvolumes are essential for creating snapshots. Use btrfs subvol snapshot to generate read-only copies.

Creating a Snapshot: 

sudo btrfs subvol snapshot -r /mnt/btrfs/data_home /mnt/btrfs/data_home_snapshot
The -r flag ensures the snapshot is read-only.

Restoring from a Snapshot: Unmount the original subvolume and replace it with the snapshot: 

sudo umount /mnt/btrfs/data_home
sudo mount -o subvol=data_home_snapshot /dev/sdb1 /mnt/btrfs_mount

docs.title: Permissions and Access Control
docs.text:
Subvolumes inherit standard Unix permissions but can be isolated for security. Use chown or chmod to adjust ownership and access rights. For granular control, combine subvolumes with Access Control Lists (ACLs): 

sudo setfacl -m u:admin:rwx /mnt/btrfs/data_home

docs.title: Troubleshooting Tips
docs.text:
• Permission Errors: Ensure the user has execute permissions on the parent directory of the subvolume.
  • Snapshot Failures: Verify the source subvolume exists and the target path is writable.
  • Mount Issues: Check if the subvolume ID matches the one in /etc/fstab or the mount command.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Subvolumes enable logical organization and independent management of Btrfs data.
  • Use btrfs subvol create and btrfs subvol snapshot for structured storage workflows.
  • Mount subvolumes via mount -o subvol=... or /etc/fstab for persistent access.
  • Snapshots on subvolumes simplify backups and rollbacks.
  • Permissions and ACLs can isolate subvolumes for security or access control.

docs.title: Variables & Scope
docs.text: Bash variables are fundamental to scripting, allowing dynamic data storage and manipulation. Understanding how to declare variables and manage their scope is critical for writing robust, maintainable scripts. Variables in Bash are untyped and assigned using the = operator, but their scope—global or local—determines where they can be accessed. Proper scoping prevents unintended side effects and namespace pollution, especially in complex scripts.

docs.title: Declaration Basics
docs.text: Variables are declared by assigning a value using the = operator. No spaces are allowed around the equals sign. By default, all variables are global, meaning they are accessible throughout the entire script and any functions.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: variable_name=value

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Simple assignment
count=0
message="Hello, World!"

# Using variables in commands
echo "Current count: $count"

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Use lowercase or mixed case (e.g., user_name).
  • Avoid uppercase unless the variable is intended to be an environment variable (e.g., API_KEY).
  • Variables are case-sensitive: USER ≠ user.

docs.title: Scope: Global vs Local
docs.text: Bash variables are global by default, but you can limit their scope using the local keyword within functions. Local variables are only accessible within the function they’re declared in, preventing unintended interactions with other parts of the script.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text:
# Global variable
global_var="I am global"

my_function() {
    echo "Inside function: $global_var"
}

my_function
echo "Outside function: $global_var"

Output: 

Inside function: I am global
Outside function: I am global

docs.title: Local Variables
docs.text:
my_function() {
    local local_var="I am local"
    echo "Inside function: $local_var"
}

my_function
echo "Outside function: $local

Output: 

Inside function: I am local
Outside function:

Attempting to access local_var outside the function results in an empty string or error, depending on context.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Prefer local in functions to avoid polluting the global namespace.
  2. Use uppercase for environment variables (e.g., MAX_RETRIES=5) to distinguish them from script variables.
  3. Avoid global variables in large scripts unless necessary; they can lead to hard-to-debug conflicts.
  4. Always quote variables when using them in commands to prevent word splitting and globbing: echo "Value: $var".

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Variables are untyped and assigned with =, with no spaces allowed.
  • Global variables are accessible throughout the script, while local restricts scope to functions.
  • Use local inside functions to prevent unintended side effects.
  • Follow naming conventions (e.g., uppercase for environment variables) for clarity.
  • Prefer local variables in larger scripts to maintain clean, modular code.

docs.title: Creating Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays can be created explicitly, assigned from command output, or built using loops.

Explicit Declaration 

fruits=(apple banana cherry)

Command Output Assignment 

mapfile -t fruits < <(some-command)

Loop-Based Construction 

while read line; do fruits+=($line); done < input.txt

docs.title: Indexing and Accessing Elements
docs.text:
Elements are accessed via zero-based indices. Negative indices reference from the end (e.g., -1 is the last element), available in BASH 4.0+. Use ${#array[@]} to get the length.

Example: Accessing elements 

echo "${fruits[0]}"        # Output: apple
echo "${fruits[-1]}"       # Output: cherry
echo "Array length: ${#fruits[@]}"  # Output: 3

docs.title: Iterating Over Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays can be iterated by elements or indices.

Element-Based Iteration 

for fruit in "${fruits[@]}"; do echo "$fruit"; done

Index-Based Iteration 

for i in $(seq 0 $(( ${#fruits[@]} -1 ))); do echo "${fruits[$i]}"; done

docs.title: Concatenation and Slicing
docs.text:
Arrays can be concatenated or sliced for subarray extraction.

Concatenation 

combined=(${fruits[@]} ${vegetables[@]})

Slicing 

echo "${fruits[@]:1:2}"   # Output: banana cherry

docs.title: Array Creation Methods
docs.text: Arrays can be created explicitly, via command output, or built with loops.

docs.title: Indexing and Length
docs.text: Use zero-based indexing, negative indices for reverse access (BASH 4.0+), and ${#array[@]} to get the length.

docs.title: Iteration Techniques
docs.text: Iterate by elements using for fruit in "${array[@]}" or by indices with seq and array indices.

docs.title: Concatenation and Slicing
docs.text: Concatenate arrays using += or array expansion, and slice with ${array[@]:start:length}.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text: Be cautious of word splitting and quoting when using command substitution to avoid unintended behavior.

docs.title: Special Parameters
docs.text: --- CURRENT PAGE --- In BASH scripting, special variables and parameters provide critical access to command-line arguments, script metadata, and runtime context. These tools are essential for building robust scripts that interact with user input and system state.

docs.title: Positional Parameters: $@ and $*
docs.text:
Positional parameters represent command-line arguments passed to a script. While both $@ and $* access all arguments, their behavior differs in expansion:

  • $@: Treats each argument as a separate string, preserving spaces within arguments. Ideal for iterating over arguments safely.
  • $*: Expands to a single string with all arguments concatenated, using the first character of IFS (typically a space) as the delimiter. Less safe for arguments with spaces.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
echo "Arguments as \$@:"
for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "$arg"
done

echo "Arguments as \$*:"
echo "$*"

Output (with input hello world 42): 

Arguments as $@:
hello
world
42
Arguments as $*:
hello world 42

docs.title: $0 - Script Name
docs.text: Represents the name of the script or the first argument passed to a function. Useful for logging or debugging.

docs.title: $? - Exit Status
docs.text: Stores the exit code of the last command executed. A return value of 0 indicates success, non-zero values indicate errors.

docs.title: $- - Option Flags
docs.text: Shows the current shell options (e.g., i for interactive mode, x for debug mode). Use with caution, as it may vary between shells.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
ls /nonexistent && echo "Success" || echo "Failure"
echo "Last command exit code: $?"
echo "Script name: $0"

Output: 

ls: /nonexistent: No such file or directory
Failure
Last command exit code: 2
Script name: script.sh

docs.title: Accessing Arguments
docs.text:
• $1, $2, ... $9: Access individual arguments (note: $10+ require indirect expansion).
  • $#: Returns the number of positional arguments.

docs.title: Example: Argument Count
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
echo "Number of arguments: $#"

Output (with input arg1 arg2): 

Number of arguments: 2

docs.title: Parsing Options with getopts
docs.text: For complex argument parsing, use getopts to handle flags and options. This avoids issues with positional parameters and ensures consistent behavior.

docs.title: Example: getopts Usage
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
while getopts "f:o:" opt; do
    case $opt in
        f) filename="$OPTARG" ;;
        o) output="$OPTARG" ;;
        \?) echo "Invalid option: -$opt" >&2 ;;
    esac
done
echo "Filename: $filename, Output: $output"

Usage: 

./script.sh -f input.txt -o output.log

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use $@ for safe iteration over arguments, and $* for concatenated strings.
  • $0 identifies the script name, while $? tracks exit codes for error handling.
  • $- reveals shell options but is rarely used in practice.
  • Always validate argument counts ($#) and use getopts for structured option parsing. --- END CURRENT PAGE ---

docs.title: Conditionals
