This generates a authkey file in /etc/corosync/. Copy this file to all cluster nodes and ensure permissions are set to 600.

docs.title: Configuring Authentication
docs.text:
Update /etc/corosync/corosync.conf: 

[totem]
    transport: tcp
    interface: 192.168.1.0/24
    auth: hmac
    authkey: /etc/corosync/authkey
- Replace authkey with the actual path to your key file. - Ensure the key file is identical across all nodes and has strict permissions.

docs.title: Node Discovery Configuration
docs.text: Corosync discovers nodes via multicast (preferred) or unicast (explicit IP listing). Multicast simplifies setup but requires a multicast-capable network.

docs.title: Multicast Discovery
docs.text:
Configure multicast in /etc/corosync/corosync.conf: 

[totem]
    transport: tcp
    interface: 192.168.1.0/24
    mcastaddr: 239.1.1.1
    mcastport: 5405
    ringnumber: 0
    bindnetaddr: 192.168.1.0
- ringnumber defines the multicast ring (use 0 for default). - bindnetaddr restricts communication to the specified subnet.

docs.title: Unicast Discovery
docs.text:
For unicast, explicitly list all nodes in the nodes section: 

[cluster]
    node: node1
    node: node2
    node: node3
- Ensure all nodes are reachable via TCP and have consistent IP addresses.

docs.title: Post-Configuration Steps
docs.text:
1. Validate Configuration: 

    sudo corosync-configure --verify
    This checks for syntax errors and connectivity issues.

  2. Restart Corosync: 

    sudo systemctl restart corosync
    Ensure the service starts without errors: 
    sudo systemctl status corosync

  3. Verify Cluster Status: Use crm_mon or pcs status to confirm nodes are communicating and the cluster is active.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Transport: Use TCP for reliability or UDP for low-latency multicast networks.
  • Authentication: Always enable hmac or sha1 with a shared authkey file.
  • Node Discovery: Prefer multicast for simplicity, but use unicast if multicast is unavailable.
  • Consistency: Ensure all nodes have identical corosync.conf and authkey files.
  • Testing: Validate configurations with corosync-configure and monitor cluster health post-deployment.

docs.title: Securing Corosync
docs.text: Corosync communication must be secured to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and unauthorized access in a high-availability cluster. This section outlines best practices for encrypting Corosync traffic, implementing authentication, and configuring firewalls to protect cluster node communication.

docs.title: TLS Encryption for Corosync
docs.text: Corosync supports Transport Layer Security (TLS) to encrypt node-to-node communication. This prevents sensitive data (e.g., authentication tokens, cluster state) from being intercepted over the network.

docs.title: 1. Generate TLS Certificates
docs.text:
Use OpenSSL to create a Certificate Authority (CA), server certificates, and private keys. Example commands: 

# Generate CA key and certificate
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048
openssl req -new -x509 -days 365 -key ca.key -out ca.crt

# Generate server key and CSR
openssl genrsa -out node.key 2048
openssl req -new -key node.key -out node.csr

# Sign CSR with CA
openssl x509 -req -in node.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out node.crt -days 365

docs.title: 2. Configure Corosync for TLS
docs.text:
Edit /etc/corosync/corosync.conf to enable TLS: 

totem {
    version: 2
    secauth: on
    tls_reject_unencrypted: yes
    tls_certificate: /etc/corosync/node.crt
    tls_key: /etc/corosync/node.key
    tls_ca_certificate: /etc/coros,ync/ca.crt
}
Ensure all nodes share the same CA certificate and use consistent paths for certificates.

docs.title: Authentication Mechanisms
docs.text: Corosync uses authentication tokens to verify node identities. Choose a method based on security and compatibility requirements:

docs.title: 1. none (Insecure, Not Recommended)
docs.text: Disables authentication entirely. Only use in trusted, isolated networks.

docs.title: 2. md5/sha1 (Legacy, Weak)
docs.text:
Uses pre-shared secret keys. Configure in corosync.conf: 

authentication {
    name: sha1
    keyfile: /etc/corosync/auth.key
}
The keyfile must be identical across all nodes and protected with strict permissions (600).

docs.title: 3. htpasswd (Recommended)
docs.text:
Uses HTTP Basic Auth-style passwords. Create a password file: 

htpasswd -c /etc/corosync/cluster.passwd node1
htpasswd /etc/corosync/cluster.passwd node2
Configure corosync.conf: 
authentication {
    name: htpasswd
    file: /etc/corosync/cluster.passwd
}
Set file permissions: chmod 600 /etc/corosync/cluster.passwd.

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text: Allow Corosync traffic through the firewall. By default, Corosync uses UDP port 5405. Update your firewall rules accordingly:

docs.title: Example: iptables
docs.text:
iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 5405 -s <node_ip> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 5405 -d <node_ip> -j ACCEPT

docs.title: Example: firewalld
docs.text:
firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="<node_ip>" port port=5405 protocol=udp accept' --permanent
firewall-cmd --reload

If TLS is enabled, ensure the firewall allows traffic on the same port (encryption occurs at the transport layer).

docs.title: Verification and Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Test Configuration: After changes, run corosync -V to validate syntax and corosync status to check connectivity.
  2. Monitor Logs: Check /var/log/corosync/corosync.log for TLS handshake failures or authentication errors.
  3. Regular Renewals: Rotate TLS certificates and passwords periodically to mitigate long-term key exposure risks.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• TLS encryption protects Corosync traffic from eavesdropping by encrypting data in transit.
  • Authentication tokens (e.g., htpasswd) ensure only trusted nodes join the cluster.
  • Firewall rules must allow UDP traffic on port 5405 (or custom port) to enable node communication.
  • Always secure certificate and password files with strict permissions (600) and rotate credentials regularly.

docs.title: Pacemaker Resources
docs.text: Pacemaker Resource Management is central to ensuring high availability and reliability in clustered environments. It involves defining, organizing, and controlling resources (services, storage, networks) to maintain their availability across cluster nodes. This section explains how Pacemaker manages resources through resource agents, constraints, and failover policies.

docs.title: Resource Agents
docs.text:
Resource agents are the core components that encapsulate the logic for managing specific services or resources. They abstract the details of starting, stopping, and monitoring resources, allowing Pacemaker to interact with them uniformly.

Key Concepts: - Standard Agents: Provided by clusters like Corosync or OpenAIS (e.g., apache, mysql, ocfs2). - External Agents: Third-party tools like heartbeat or drbd can also be integrated. - Agent Metadata: Each agent has metadata (e.g., CIB schema) describing its capabilities (e.g., start, stop, monitor).

Example: Creating a Resource 

pcs resource create apache systemd:apache
This command creates a resource named apache using the systemd agent for the apache2 service.

Managing Resources: Use pcs or crm_resource to manipulate resources: 

pcs resource disable apache  # Temporarily stop the resource
pcs resource enable apache   # Restart the resource
crm_resource --resource apache --action status  # Check resource status

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints define relationships between resources and nodes, ensuring predictable behavior during failures.

Types of Constraints: 1. Location Constraints: Specify where a resource should run. 

pcs constraint location apache prefers node1=100
This ensures the apache resource prefers to run on node1.

  1. Order Constraints: Define dependencies between resources. 

    pcs constraint order start mysql then start apache
    The mysql resource must start before apache.

  2. Colocation Constraints: Enforce co-location of resources. 

    pcs constraint colocation add mysql apache
    The apache resource must run on the same node as mysql.

Note: Constraints are critical for avoiding split-brain scenarios and ensuring service dependencies are met.

docs.title: Failover Policies
docs.text:
Failover policies determine how Pacemaker handles resource failures and node outages.

Stonith Policies: - stonith-symmetric: Nodes can take over resources after a STONITH (shoot node) action. - stonith-asymmetric: Only the surviving node can take over resources.

Failure Policy: The failure-policy attribute defines how Pacemaker responds to node failures: - reconnect: Attempt to reconnect to the failed node. - stop: Stop resources if the node fails.

Example: Configuring Failover Policies 

pcs resource defaults failure-policy=stop
pcs resource defaults stonith-symmetric=true
These settings ensure resources stop if a node fails and enable symmetric STONITH behavior.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Resource agents abstract service management, enabling uniform control across diverse services.
  • Constraints (location, order, colocation) ensure predictable resource placement and dependencies.
  • Failover policies (STONITH modes, failure handling) dictate how resources are managed during node failures.
  • Tools like pcs and crm_resource are essential for configuring and monitoring resources.
  • Proper resource management minimizes downtime and ensures cluster resilience.

docs.title: Resource Groups
docs.text: Pacemaker resources represent the services, IP addresses, or filesystems that your cluster manages to ensure high availability. Defining and managing these resources is critical to configuring a resilient cluster. This section provides step-by-step guidance for creating and managing resources using the pcs (Pacemaker Cluster Suite) command-line tool.

docs.title: Service Resources
docs.text:
To define a service resource, use the pcs resource create command with the service name and the underlying systemd unit. For example, to create a resource for Apache:

pcs resource create apache systemd:apache

This creates a resource named apache that starts the apache2 service. You can verify its existence with:

pcs resource show

docs.title: IP Address Resources
docs.text:
IP address resources ensure a consistent IP address is available across cluster nodes. Use the IPaddr2 resource agent:

pcs resource create virtual_ip ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 ip=192.168.1.100 interface=eth0

This creates a resource named virtual_ip that manages the IP address 192.168.1.100 on the eth0 interface. Adjust the IP and interface as needed.

docs.title: Filesystem Resources
docs.text:
Filesystems are managed using the Filesystem resource agent. Define a resource to mount a shared filesystem:

pcs resource create shared_fs ocf:heartbeat:Filesystem device=/dev/sdb1 directory=/mnt/shared options=rw

This mounts the /dev/sdb1 device to /mnt/shared with read-write permissions. Ensure the device and mount point match your storage configuration.

docs.title: Starting and Stopping Resources
docs.text:
Use pcs resource start and pcs resource stop to control individual resources:

pcs resource start apache
pcs resource stop virtual_ip

To stop all resources on a node, use:

pcs resource stop --all

docs.title: Migrating Resources
docs.text:
Move a resource to a specific node with:

pcs resource move apache node2

This ensures the apache service runs on node2. To force a migration, add the --force flag:

pcs resource move apache node2 --force

docs.title: Checking Resource Status
docs.text:
Use pcs status to view the current state of all resources and their locations:

pcs status

This output shows which node hosts each resource and whether they are online or offline.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Use pcs resource create to define services, IP addresses, and filesystems with appropriate resource agents.
  • Manage resources with pcs resource start, stop, move, and disable commands.
  • Always verify resource status with pcs status to ensure proper cluster behavior.
  • Test migrations and failover scenarios to validate resource resilience.

docs.title: Colocation Rules
docs.text: Pacemaker resource groups and colocation constraints are essential for managing interdependent resources and ensuring coordinated failover in a high-availability cluster. By grouping related resources and defining colocation rules, you enforce logical dependencies that prevent partial failures and maintain service continuity during node outages.

docs.title: Resource Groups: Bundling Interdependent Resources
docs.text: A resource group is a logical container for one or more resources that should be managed as a single unit. This ensures that all resources within the group are started, stopped, and migrated together, preserving application consistency.

docs.title: Creating a Resource Group
docs.text:
To create a resource group, use the crm configure command and define it in the cluster configuration. For example: 

crm configure primitive web_server ocf:heartbeat:HTTP \
  params port=80 \
  op start timeout=20s \
  op stop timeout=20s

crm configure primitive shared_fs ocf:heartbeat:Filesystem \
  params device="/dev/sdb" directory="/var/www" \
  op start timeout=20s \
  op stop timeout=203

crm configure group web_group web_server shared_fs

This groups the web_server and shared_fs resources, ensuring they move together during failover.

docs.title: Verifying the Group
docs.text:
Use crm configure show to inspect the group structure: 

crm configure show | grep -A 5 'group'
Output will include the group definition and its member resources.

docs.title: Colocation Constraints: Enforcing Node-Level Dependencies
docs.text: Colocation constraints ensure that specific resources (or groups) are scheduled on the same node. This is critical for dependencies where one resource requires another to be active, such as a database needing a shared storage resource.

docs.title: Defining a Colocation Constraint
docs.text:
To colocate a resource group with another resource, use the <colocation> element in the configuration. For example: 

crm configure colocation web_group_with_storage \
  score=INFINITY \
  resource=web_group \
  rsc=storage_resource

This ensures the web_group is always placed on the same node as storage_resource. The score=INFINITY enforces a hard requirement, while lower scores allow flexibility.

docs.title: Example Use Case
docs.text:
If a database resource (db_resource) depends on a shared storage resource (storage_resource), you might colocate them: 

crm configure colocation db_with_storage \
  score=INFINITY \
  resource=db_resource \
  rsc=storage_resource

docs.title: Best Practices for Resource Groups and Colocation
docs.text:
1. Group tightly coupled resources (e.g., application + database + filesystem) to avoid partial failures.
  2. Use colocation for critical dependencies (e.g., ensuring a database runs only on nodes with attached storage).
  3. Balance colocation scores to avoid over-constraining the cluster while meeting operational needs.
  4. Test failover scenarios to validate that grouped resources and colocation rules behave as expected.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Resource groups bundle interdependent resources for unified management during failover.
  • Colocation constraints ensure resources (or groups) are scheduled on the same node, preserving application integrity.
  • Proper grouping and colocation rules prevent partial failures and improve cluster reliability.
  • Always validate configurations with crm configure show and test failover scenarios.

docs.title: STONITH Concepts
docs.text: High Availability Clusters rely on mechanisms to prevent split-brain scenarios—situations where network partitions cause multiple nodes to independently assume ownership of shared resources. STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) is a critical fencing mechanism designed to isolate faulty or unreachable nodes, ensuring data consistency and preventing resource conflicts. By forcibly disconnecting problematic nodes from the cluster, STONITH safeguards the integrity of shared storage and services.

docs.title: Split-Brain Prevention
docs.text: Split-brain occurs when a cluster's communication network splits into isolated partitions. Without fencing, nodes in separate partitions may independently claim resources (e.g., a shared disk), leading to data corruption or service outages. STONITH prevents this by: 1. Isolating nodes that fail to respond to heartbeat signals. 2. Forcing a single point of control to determine which node(s) are safe to operate. 3. Preventing resource duplication by ensuring only one node can access critical resources at a time.

docs.title: Fencing Mechanisms
docs.text:
STONITH leverages hardware or software-based fencing agents to isolate nodes. Common mechanisms include: - IPMI ( Intelligent Platform Management Interface): Uses out-of-band management to power cycle or reboot nodes. - Power Switches: Physically disconnects nodes via serial or network-connected power outlets (e.g., APC UPS). - SSH: Executes commands on a node to terminate processes or reboot. - FCP (Fibre Channel over Ethernet): Disconnects nodes from shared storage.

Each mechanism requires specific configuration to ensure it can reach and act on the target node. For example, an IPMI-based fence device might be configured with: 

pcs fence device add ipmi1 ipmi_host=192.168.1.100 ipmi_user=admin ipmi_password=secret

docs.title: Fencing Process
docs.text:
The fencing process is triggered when a node fails to respond to cluster heartbeats. Pacemaker evaluates the node's status and applies fencing policies defined in the cluster configuration. Key steps include: 1. Detection: A node is marked unreachable after multiple failed heartbeat checks. 2. Decision: The cluster determines if fencing is necessary (e.g., based on quorum rules). 3. Execution: The appropriate fencing agent isolates the node (e.g., power cycling it or disconnecting its storage access).

Fencing policies must explicitly define which nodes can be fenced and the order of operations. For example: 

pcs constraint location node1 -inf: fence=off
pcs constraint location node2 -inf: fence=on

docs.title: Configuration Examples
docs.text:
To verify fencing status and test configurations: 

pcs status | grep 'Fencing'
# Output: Fencing: fence=on (node2), fence=off (node1)

To test a fencing action (use with caution): 

pcs cluster enable --all
pcs cluster stop node2
pcs cluster start node2

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• STONITH is essential for preventing split-brain by isolating faulty nodes.
  • Fencing mechanisms vary by hardware/software and require explicit configuration.
  • Fencing policies must define node isolation rules and priorities.
  • Regular testing and monitoring ensure fencing actions work reliably during failures.
  • Always validate fencing configurations in a safe environment before production use.

docs.title: Fencing Devices
docs.text: Pacemaker relies on STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) devices to ensure data consistency by isolating failed nodes in a cluster. Proper configuration of STONITH devices is critical to prevent split-brain scenarios and ensure reliable failover. This section guides you through discovering, configuring, and validating STONITH devices in a Pacemaker cluster.

docs.title: Discovering and Configuring STONITH Devices
docs.text: Before configuring a STONITH device, you must first identify supported agents using the pcs stonith discover command. This command lists available STONITH agents, not network devices. Use agent-specific discovery tools for network devices.

docs.title: Example: Listing Available STONITH Agents
docs.text:
pcs stonith discover
Output might include: 
ipmi
apc

docs.title: Example: Discovering IPMI-based STONITH Devices
docs.text:
Use fence_ipmi -d for IPMI device discovery: 

fence_ipmi -d
Output might include: 
IPMI device found at: 192.168.1.100

docs.title: Example: Discovering APC UPS Devices
docs.text:
Use fence_apcups -d for APC device discovery: 

fence_apcups -d
Output might include: 
APC device found at: 192.168.1.200

Once discovered, configure the device using pcs stonith add. Parameters depend on the STONITH agent.

docs.title: Example: Configuring an IPMI Device
docs.text:
pcs stonith add ipmi-01 ipmi \
  --ipaddr=192.168.1.100 \
  --username=admin \
  --password=securepassword \
  --chassis-type=blade

docs.title: Example: Configuring an APC UPS
docs.text:
pcs stonith add apc-01 apc \
  --ipaddr=192.168.1.200 \
  --username=admin \
  --password=securepassword

Note: For IP-based fencing (e.g., fence_ipmi), ensure the device IP is reachable from all cluster nodes and that firewall rules allow communication on the required port (typically 6666 for IPMI).

docs.title: Defining Fencing Policies
docs.text: Pacemaker uses the stonith resource to define fencing policies. These policies determine how and when nodes are fenced. Configure stonith resources using pcs commands, not manual XML editing.

docs.title: Example: Defining a STONITH Resource
docs.text:
pcs stonith add ipmi-01 ipmi \
  --ipaddr=192.168.1.100 \
  --username=admin \
  --password=securepassword \
  --chassis-type=blade

docs.title: Key Fencing Policy Parameters
docs.text:
• stonith-action: Specifies the fencing method (e.g., reboot, off, poweroff).
  • reboot-node: Enables node reboot after fencing (useful for IPMI).
  • fail-count: Number of consecutive failures before fencing is triggered.
  • timeout: Timeout in seconds for fencing operations.

Example configuration with parameters: 

pcs stonith update ipmi-01 \
  --stonith-action=reboot \
  --fail-count=3 \
  --timeout=30

docs.title: Cluster-Wide Fencing Level
docs.text:
Set the fencing-level via stonith resource properties: 

pcs stonith update ipmi-01 \
  --fencing-level=strict
- strict: Fences nodes only if they are unreachable. - normal: Fences nodes if they are suspected of failing. - none: Disables fencing (not recommended).

docs.title: Testing STONITH Configuration
docs.text: After configuring STONITH devices, validate the setup to ensure it works as expected.

docs.title: Example: Verifying Fencing Configuration
docs.text:
pcs cluster verify
This command checks for syntax errors in the cluster configuration.

docs.title: Example: Simulating a Node Failure
docs.text:
pcs node disable <node-name>
This simulates a node failure and triggers the fencing policy. Monitor the output to confirm the STONITH device isolates the node.

docs.title: Example: Checking Fencing Logs
docs.text:
journalctl -u pacemaker -n 50
Review logs for errors during fencing operations, such as authentication failures or network issues.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use pcs stonith discover to identify supported STONITH agents. Use agent-specific tools (e.g., fence_ipmi -d) for network device discovery.
  • Configure devices with pcs stonith add, specifying parameters like IP, credentials, and chassis type.
  • Define fencing policies via the stonith resource, adjusting stonith-action, fail-count, and timeout as needed.
  • Test fencing with pcs cluster verify and simulated node failures to ensure reliability.
  • Regularly monitor logs with journalctl to troubleshoot fencing-related issues.

docs.title: Validating Fencing
docs.text: Testing and Validating Fencing is a critical step in ensuring the reliability of a Pacemaker cluster. Fencing mechanisms (STONITH) must be verified to ensure they can isolate failed nodes and prevent data corruption or split-brain scenarios. This section outlines methods to simulate node failures, validate fencing behavior, and confirm the effectiveness of your STONITH configuration.

docs.title: Simulating Node Failures
docs.text: To test fencing, simulate node failures without disrupting production workloads. Use the following approaches:

docs.title: 1. Use pcs cluster simulate
docs.text:
Simulate a node failure by triggering a simulated failure scenario: 

pcs cluster simulate <node>
Monitor the cluster response using crm_mon -l to observe if the cluster detects the failure and initiates fencing. For virtual machines, you can also simulate a crash by: 
pcs cluster simulate <node>
Ensure the cluster isolates the node and transitions it to a fenced state.

docs.title: 2. Test STONITH Devices Directly
docs.text:
Use the stonith_admin utility to test fencing devices: 

sudo stonith_admin -t <stonith_device_name>
Replace <stonith_device_name> with your actual fencing device (e.g., fence_xvm for VMs). This command verifies the device's ability to power off or isolate a node.

docs.title: Verifying Fencing Effectiveness
docs.text: After simulating failures, validate that the cluster correctly isolates nodes and maintains quorum:

docs.title: 1. Check Cluster Status
docs.text:
Use crm_mon -l to confirm the cluster's state. A properly fenced node should appear in a fenced state, and the cluster should retain quorum: 

Node 1: online
Node 2: fenced

docs.title: 2. Inspect STONITH Device Status
docs.text:
Verify the STONITH device's operational status: 

pcs stonith status
Ensure the device reports online and has no pending errors.

docs.title: 3. Review Logs
docs.text:
Check logs for fencing-related events: 

journalctl -u pacemaker --since "1 hour ago"
Look for entries like stonith-action or fence_xvm to confirm fencing actions were executed.

docs.title: Best Practices for Fencing Testing
docs.text:
• Avoid Production Systems: Test in a staging environment or isolated VMs to prevent unintended outages.
  • Document Scenarios: Record test cases and results to identify edge cases or configuration gaps.
  • Validate Device Compatibility: Ensure fencing devices are supported by your cluster version (e.g., IPMI, power management tools).
  • Test Recovery: After fencing, verify the node can rejoin the cluster by restarting its services: 
    sudo systemctl start pacemaker

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Simulate node failures using pcs cluster simulate or direct STONITH testing to validate fencing behavior.
  • Monitor cluster status with crm_mon and check STONITH device logs to confirm isolation success.
  • Always test in non-production environments to avoid disruptions.
  • Regularly validate fencing configurations to ensure resilience against hardware or software failures.
  • Document test outcomes to refine STONITH policies and improve cluster reliability.

docs.title: Virtual IP Config
docs.text: High Availability (HA) clusters often rely on virtual IP addresses (VIPs) to ensure services remain accessible even when individual nodes fail. A VIP acts as a shared, floating IP address that the cluster manages, allowing clients to connect to services without needing to know the underlying node's IP. This section explains how to configure and manage VIPs in a Pacemaker-based cluster.

docs.title: Planning Your VIP Configuration
docs.text: Before configuring a VIP, consider these factors: - Subnet isolation: Assign the VIP to a dedicated subnet (e.g., 192.168.100.0/24) to avoid conflicts with node IPs. - Network interface: Ensure all cluster nodes have a physical or virtual interface connected to the VIP subnet. - Failover priority: Define which nodes should own the VIP during normal operation (e.g., using stonith or fence devices for failover).

docs.title: Configuring the VIP on the Operating System
docs.text:
Each node must have the VIP assigned to its network interface. Use ip or nmcli to configure this. For example: 

# Assign VIP to eth0 on node1
sudo ip addr add 192.168.100.10/24 dev eth0
sudo ip link set eth0 up
Verify the interface is active: 
ip addr show eth0

docs.title: Adding the VIP to Pacemaker
docs.text:
Use pcs to create a VIP resource. Replace 192.168.100.10 with your VIP and node1 with the primary node: 

pcs resource create VIP IPaddr2 \
  ip=192.163.100.10 \
  cidr_netmask=24 \
  nic=eth0 \
  op monitor interval=30s
This creates a resource named VIP that manages the IP address. Ensure the resource is started: 
pcs status

docs.title: Managing VIP Failover
docs.text:
Pacemaker automatically moves the VIP to a healthy node during failover. To test: 1. Simulate node failure: 

sudo systemctl stop corosync
2. Check VIP ownership: 
ip addr show eth0 | grep "inet\|inet6"
The VIP should now be on the secondary node.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Common Issues
docs.text:
• VIP not assigned: Ensure the interface is up and the subnet is correctly configured.
  • Failover not working: Check stonith configuration and ensure nodes are reachable via fencing.
  • Conflicts with static routes: Use ip route to verify routing tables if the VIP is on a different subnet.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• VIPs provide a stable endpoint for HA services, abstracting node-specific IP addresses.
  • Configure VIPs on all cluster nodes and assign them to a dedicated subnet.
  • Use pcs to manage VIP resources, ensuring they are monitored and failover-ready.
  • Test failover scenarios to validate VIP migration and network resilience.
  • Always isolate VIP subnets to avoid conflicts and ensure predictable routing.

docs.title: VIP Failover
docs.text: High Availability Clusters often rely on a Virtual IP (VIP) to provide a stable endpoint for clients, even when nodes fail or migrate. Automating VIP failover with Pacemaker ensures seamless transitions between nodes, maintaining service availability. This section details how to configure and manage VIP failover using Pacemaker resources and CRM commands.

docs.title: Configuring VIP as a Pacemaker Resource
docs.text:
To automate VIP failover, define the VIP as a resource in Pacemaker using the ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 agent (or a compatible agent). This resource manages the IP address and ensures it moves to a healthy node during failover.

Example: Define a VIP resource 

crm configure primitive VIP_IP ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 \
  params ip="192.168.1.100" cidr_netmask="24" \
  op monitor interval="30s" timeout="20s"

Key parameters: - ip: The VIP address to manage. - cidr_netmask: Subnet mask (e.g., 24 for /24 network). - network: Optional, specifies the network interface (e.g., eth0).

docs.title: Ensuring Service Dependencies and Ordering
docs.text:
The VIP must be fenced properly to avoid split-brain scenarios. Use stonith (fencing) to isolate failed nodes. Additionally, ensure services depend on the VIP being online before starting.

Example: Enforce VIP availability before service start 

crm configure order start-vip-before-services \
  inferschema=true \
  then="VIP_IP" \
  then="apache"

This ensures the VIP resource is online before starting the apache service.

docs.title: Monitoring and Testing VIP Failover
docs.text:
Use crm_mon -1 to monitor the cluster state and verify VIP placement. Simulate a node failure to test failover: 

pcs cluster stop node1

Observe the VIP migrating to a healthy node. Validate connectivity to the VIP and ensure services remain operational.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Define VIP as a Pacemaker resource using ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 to automate failover.
  • Enforce ordering constraints to ensure services depend on the VIP being online.
  • Test failover scenarios with pcs cluster stop and use crm_mon to verify VIP migration.
  • Integrate fencing (stonith) to prevent split-brain and ensure node isolation.
  • Monitor cluster status regularly to confirm VIP and service availability.

docs.title: Network Resilience
docs.text: High availability clusters rely on robust network resilience to ensure continuous operation during failures. Network resilience strategies must address both physical and logical redundancy, ensuring that nodes and virtual IP addresses (VIPs) remain accessible even when individual network components fail. This section outlines best practices for designing resilient network architectures in Pacemaker-based clusters.

docs.title: Multi-Homed Node Configuration
docs.text: Multi-homed nodes (nodes with multiple network interfaces) provide redundancy by allowing traffic to route through alternative paths. This is critical for maintaining connectivity during partial network outages.

docs.title: Example: Configuring Multiple Network Interfaces
docs.text:
# Assign multiple IPs to a single interface (e.g., eth1)
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth1
sudo ip addr add 192.168.2.10/24 dev eth1

# Verify configuration
ip addr show eth1

docs.title: Bonding/Teaming for Redundancy
docs.text:
Bonding (Linux) or teaming (Windows) combines multiple NICs into a single logical interface, providing failover and load balancing: 

# Example bonding configuration (eth0 and eth1)
sudo nmcli connection add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 mode active-backup
sudo nmcli connection add type bond-slave con-name bond0-slave0 ifname eth0 master bond0
sudo nmcli connection add type bond-slave con-name bond0-slave1 ifname eth1 master bond0

docs.title: Redundant VIP Configuration
docs.text: Virtual IP addresses (VIPs) must be configured redundantly across cluster nodes to avoid single points of failure. Use multiple VIPs or assign VIPs to different subnets for added resilience.

docs.title: Example: Assigning VIPs to Multiple Nodes
docs.text:
# Assign VIP to node1
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.20/24 dev eth1

# Assign VIP to node2
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.20/24 dev eth1

docs.title: Pacemaker Resource Configuration
docs.text:
Ensure VIPs are managed by Pacemaker to handle failover automatically: 

<resources>
  <ip addr="192.168.1.20" name="vip-1"/>
  <ip addr="192.168.2.20" name="vip-2"/>
</resources>

docs.title: Cross-Subnet and ISP Diversity
docs.text: Deploy VIPs across different subnets or ISPs to mitigate risks of localized outages. For example, use a VIP in a public subnet for external access and a private VIP for internal services.

docs.title: Additional Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Regular Failover Testing: Simulate network failures using tools like ipfail or keepalived to validate failover behavior.
  2. Network Monitoring: Integrate tools like nagios or Prometheus to monitor interface status, latency, and packet loss.
  3. Redundant Routing Protocols: Use protocols like VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) to manage default gateways across nodes.
  4. Firewall Rules: Ensure firewalls allow traffic between cluster nodes and VIPs, with rules prioritizing failover scenarios.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Multi-homed nodes provide redundancy by using multiple NICs or bonding/teaming.
  • Redundant VIPs across nodes and subnets ensure continuous service availability.
  • Regular testing and monitoring validate network resilience in real-world scenarios.
  • Cross-subnet and ISP diversity reduces risks of localized network failures.
  • Automated failover via Pacemaker ensures VIPs transition seamlessly during outages.

docs.title: Cluster Health
docs.text: High availability clusters rely on continuous monitoring to detect failures, ensure resource availability, and maintain quorum. Tools like crm_mon, pcs status, and corosync-quorum provide critical insights into cluster health, node status, and resource assignments. Regular checks using these utilities help administrators proactively address issues before they impact service availability.

docs.title: Real-Time Cluster Status with crm_mon
docs.text: The crm_mon command provides a live view of the cluster's state, including node status, resource assignments, and fence device configurations. It is the primary tool for diagnosing cluster health during runtime.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
crm_mon -1
The -1 flag displays one line per node, showing their current status (e.g., Online, Offline, Stopped). For a detailed tree view: 
crm_mon

docs.title: Interpreting Output
docs.text:
• Node Status: Online indicates the node is operational; Offline suggests a failure or maintenance mode.
  • Resource Status: Resources like virtual IPs or services are marked as Started or Stopped.
  • Fence Devices: Indicates if fencing mechanisms are active (e.g., Fence or No Fence).

Example Output: 

Stack: corosync
Current DC: node1 (version 2.0.5-125.el7) - partition with quorum
Last updated: Thu Jul 18 14:30:00 2024
Last change: Thu Jul 18 14:25:00 2024 by root via cibadmin on node1

docs.title: Cluster Configuration and Status with pcs status
docs.text: The pcs status command provides a high-level overview of the cluster's configuration, including node status, resource placement, and lease information. It is ideal for verifying the cluster's configuration after changes.

docs.title: Key Output Sections
docs.text:
1. Cluster Status: Indicates if the cluster is active and has quorum.
  2. Node Status: Lists nodes and their current state (e.g., Online, Offline).
  3. Resources: Shows which resources are running and their assigned nodes.
  4. Leases: Displays lease information for resources, which is critical for failover.

docs.title: Example Command
docs.text:
pcs status

Example Output: 

Cluster name: mycluster
Stack: corosync
Current DC: node1 (version 2.0.5-125.el7) - partition with quorum
Last updated: Thu Jul 18 14:30:00 2024
Last change: Thu Jul 18 14:25:00 2024 by root via cibadmin on node1

Nodes:
 Online: node1 node2

Resources:
 Resource: vip-clone (ocf::heartbeat:IPaddr2): Started node1
 Resource: web-server (ocf::heartbeat:apache): Started node1

 leases:
 Resource: vip-clone: lease is active

docs.title: Quorum and Corosync Status with corosync-quorum
docs.text: Quorum ensures the cluster remains functional even if some nodes fail. The corosync-quorum tool checks the quorum status and helps diagnose split-brain scenarios.

docs.title: Checking Quorum Status
docs.text: corosync-quorumstatus

docs.title: Key Indicators
docs.text:
• Quorum Status: Quorum: 2 means two nodes are in the majority (required for cluster operation).
  • Split-Brain Detection: If nodes are partitioned, the output may show Quorum: 0 or Quorum: 1, indicating a potential split-brain scenario.

Example Output: 

Quorum: 2
Nodes: 2

docs.title: Interpreting Cluster Health
docs.text:
• Normal Operation: All nodes are Online, resources are Started, and quorum is maintained.
  • Warning Signs:
  • Nodes marked Offline or Stopped.
  • Resources in Stopped state.
  • Quorum status below the required threshold.
  • Troubleshooting Steps: Use crm_mon to identify failing resources, pcs status to verify configuration, and corosync-quorum to check for network partitions.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use crm_mon for real-time cluster state and resource tracking.
  • Run pcs status to validate configuration and resource placement.
  • Monitor quorum with corosync-quorum to prevent split-brain scenarios.
  • Regularly check node status, resource availability, and quorum health to maintain cluster reliability.

docs.title: Cluster Alerts
docs.text: Pacemaker clusters rely on timely alerts to notify administrators of critical events such as node failures, resource downtime, or configuration issues. This section covers methods to configure alerts using systemd, email, and external monitoring tools, ensuring proactive maintenance and rapid response.

docs.title: Using systemd for Cluster Alerts
docs.text:
Systemd can be leveraged to run custom scripts that monitor cluster health and trigger alerts. Create a systemd service unit to periodically check the cluster status and execute alert actions.

Example: Create a systemd service for cluster health checks 

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/cluster-alert.service
Add the following content: 
[Unit]
Description=Cluster Health Alert Service
Timer=cluster-alert.timer

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/bin/cluster-health-check.sh

Example: Define a timer to run checks every 5 minutes 

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/cluster-alert.timer
Add: 
[Unit]
Description=Run cluster health checks every 5 minutes

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*:0/5
Unit=cluster-alert.service

Example: Script to trigger alerts 

#!/bin/bash
CLUSTER_STATUS=$(crm_mon -1 | grep "stack is online")
if [[ ! $CLUSTER_STATUS ]]; then
  echo "Cluster is offline!" | mail -s "Pacemaker Alert" admin@example.com
fi
Enable and start the service: 
sudo systemctl enable --now cluster-alert.timer

docs.title: Email Alerts with mail or sendmail
docs.text:
Configure the cluster to send email notifications for critical events. Use tools like mail or sendmail to relay alerts.

Example: Script to send email alerts 

#!/bin/bash
if ! crm_mon -1 | grep -q "online"; then
  echo "CRITICAL: Cluster is offline!" | mail -s "Pacemaker Alert" admin@example.com
fi
Ensure the mail transfer agent (MTA) is installed and configured (e.g., postfix or sendmail). Note that the mail command requires an MTA to be installed and properly configured before use.

docs.title: External Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
Integrate Pacemaker with external tools like Nagios, Zabbix, or Prometheus for centralized monitoring. Use the Pacemaker REST API or SSH to query cluster status.

Example: Check cluster status via SSH 

ssh cluster-node1 "crm_mon -1 | grep 'online'"
if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then
  echo "Cluster offline on cluster-node1" | tee /path/to/alert.log
fi

Example: Nagios plugin for cluster health 

#!/bin/bash
if crm_mon -1 | grep -q "online"; then
  echo "OK"
  exit 0
else
  echo "CRITICAL: Cluster offline"
  exit 2
fi
Place this script in Nagios' plugin directory and configure checks in nagios.cfg.

docs.title: Testing and Validation
docs.text:
1. Simulate node failure: 
    pcs cluster stop node1
    Note: This command requires a multi-node cluster. For single-node setups, use alternative methods like stopping the cluster service or simulating failures through other means.
  2. Verify alerts are triggered via email, logs, or monitoring tools.
  3. Restore the node and ensure alerts resolve.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use systemd to run periodic health checks and trigger alerts via scripts.
  • Configure email alerts using mail or sendmail for quick notifications.
  • Integrate with external tools like Nagios or Zabbix for centralized monitoring.
  • Test alerts by simulating failures to ensure reliability.
  • Always validate alert configurations against your environment's specific tools and policies.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: High availability clusters require regular maintenance and proactive troubleshooting to ensure reliability. This section covers procedures for managing node downtime, migrating resources, and resolving common cluster failures using Pacemaker and related tools.

docs.title: Graceful Node Shutdowns
docs.text:
To perform maintenance on a node, first ensure all critical resources are migrated. Use pcs cluster stop to stop a node gracefully: 

pcs cluster stop <node-name>
Verify resource migration with crm_mon -1 or pcs status. After maintenance, restart the node and re-enable cluster services: 
pcs cluster start <node-name>
pcs cluster enable <node-name>

docs.title: Handling Unplanned Downtime
docs.text:
If a node fails unexpectedly, Pacemaker may trigger fencing. Check the cluster status: 

pcs status
If fencing is active, disable it temporarily to investigate: 
pcs cluster disable <node-name>
After resolving the issue, re-enable the node and rejoin the cluster.

docs.title: Moving Resources Manually
docs.text:
Use pcs resource move to relocate a resource to a specific node: 

pcs resource move <resource-id> <target-node>
Verify the move: 
pcs status
Ensure dependencies are met by checking resource constraints with pcs constraint show.

docs.title: Failover Testing
docs.text:
Simulate a node failure to test failover: 

pcs cluster stop <node-name> --force
Monitor resource migration with crm_mon -1. After testing, restore the node: 
pcs cluster start <node-name>

docs.title: Resource Failures
docs.text:
If a resource fails, check its status: 

pcs status <resource-id>
Disable the resource temporarily to investigate: 
pcs resource disable <resource-id>
After resolving the issue, re-enable it: 
pcs resource enable <resource-id>

docs.title: Communication Issues
docs.text:
Verify network connectivity between nodes: 

ping <peer-node-ip>
Check firewall rules to ensure ports (e.g., 3121 for Corosync) are open. Use pcs cluster setup to reconfigure communication if needed.

docs.title: Fencing Problems
docs.text:
If fencing fails, check the fence agent configuration: 

pcs fence show
Test fencing with: 
pcs cluster disable <node-name>
pcs cluster enable <node-name>
Review logs for errors: 
journalctl -u pacemaker

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Plan node maintenance by migrating resources and using pcs cluster stop/start.
  • Manually move resources with pcs resource move and verify with pcs status.
  • Troubleshoot failures by checking resource status, network connectivity, and fencing configurations.
  • Regularly test failover scenarios to validate cluster resilience.
  • Use logs (journalctl, pcs status) to diagnose and resolve persistent issues.

docs.title: Unit Files Syntax
docs.text: Systemd unit files are configuration files that define how services, sockets, timers, and other units should behave in a systemd-managed system. These files are written in a structured key-value format and dictate the lifecycle, dependencies, and runtime parameters for systemd units. Understanding their structure is critical for customizing and debugging systemd-based services.

docs.title: Structure of a Unit File
docs.text: A typical unit file contains multiple [Section] blocks, each defining specific aspects of the unit. The most common sections are [Unit], [Service], and [Install], though other sections like [Socket] or [Timer] exist for specialized unit types.

docs.title: [Unit] Section
docs.text:
The [Unit] section provides metadata and dependencies. Key directives include: - Description: A human-readable description of the unit. - After: Specifies units that must start before this one. - Requires: Ensures dependent units are started. - Conflicts: Defines units that cannot run simultaneously.

Example: 

[Unit]
Description=My Custom Service
After=network.target
Requires=network-online.target

docs.title: [Service] Section
docs.text:
The [Service] section defines how the service should run. Key directives include: - ExecStart: The command to start the service. - WorkingDirectory: The directory to run the service from. - Restart: Specifies restart policies (e.g., always, on-failure). - User and Group: The user and group to run the service as.

Example: 

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/myapp --flag
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
Restart=always
User=myuser
Group=mygroup

docs.title: [Install] Section
docs.text:
The [Install] section determines how the unit is linked to systemd's service management. Key directives include: - WantedBy: Specifies the target (e.g., multi-user.target) to enable the service. - Alias: Provides an alternative name for the unit.

Example: 

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Alias=myapp.service

docs.title: Socket Units
docs.text:
Socket units manage socket activation. They define how systemd should listen for connections and spawn the service when needed. Key directives include: - SocketMode: Permissions for the socket file. - ListenStream: Specifies TCP/UDP sockets. - PassThrough: Controls whether the socket is passed to the service.

Example: 

[Socket]
ListenStream=8080
SocketMode=0666
PassThrough=socket

docs.title: Timer Units
docs.text:
Timer units schedule services to run at specific intervals. They use a [Timer] section with directives like: - OnCalendar: Defines the schedule (e.g., *-*-* 12:00:00 for daily at noon). - Unit: Links the timer to a service unit.

Example: 

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Unit=myapp.service

docs.title: Managing Unit Files
docs.text:
• Viewing Unit Files: Use systemctl cat <unit-name> to inspect the contents of a unit file.
  • Overriding Defaults: Use systemctl edit <unit-name> to create override files in /etc/systemd/system/.
  • Validating Syntax: Run systemd-analyze verify <unit-file> to check for syntax errors.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Unit files define the behavior of systemd units through structured sections like [Unit], [Service], and [Install].
  • Different unit types (e.g., socket, timer) use specialized sections to manage their unique functionality.
  • Always validate unit files for syntax errors and test changes in a controlled environment.
  • Overrides and custom unit files in /etc/systemd/system/ allow fine-grained control over systemd behavior.

docs.title: Creating and Configuring Custom Systemd Service Units
Example Service Unit File
docs.text:
Create a file at /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service with the following content:

[Unit]
Description=My Custom Application Service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=myappuser
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
ExecStart=/usr/bin/gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:5000 app:app
Restart=on-failure
StandardOutput=syslog
StandardError=syslog
SyslogIdentifier=myapp

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Step-by-Step Configuration
docs.text:
1. Create the service file using nano or vim
  2. Reload systemd with sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  3. Enable the service with sudo systemctl enable myapp.service
  4. Start the service with sudo systemctl start myapp.service
  5. Verify status with systemctl status myapp.service

docs.title: Example Use Case: Web Application
docs.text: For a Python Flask app running as myappuser: - Place the service file in /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service - Set WorkingDirectory to the app's root directory - Use ExecStart with gunicorn or uvicorn as the application server: - ExecStart=/usr/bin/gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:5000 app:app - ExecStart=/usr/bin/uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 - Configure StandardOutput and StandardError for logging

docs.title: Best Practices Integration
docs.text:
• Naming: Use myapp.service for clear identification
  • Permissions: Run as dedicated user (myappuser) for security
  • Logging: Direct output to syslog with SyslogIdentifier
  • Testing: Use systemctl daemon-reload followed by systemctl status myapp.service for syntax validation
  • Restart Policy: Set Restart=on-failure for reliability

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text: Systemd unit files are the foundation of service management in Linux systems. They define how services, sockets, timers, and other units are configured, launched, and integrated into the systemd ecosystem. Mastery of their syntax and best practices ensures reliability, security, and maintainability. This section explores the structure of unit files, key best practices, and common pitfalls to avoid when authoring them.

docs.title: Core Syntax Structure
docs.text: A systemd unit file is a plaintext configuration file divided into sections and key-value pairs. Each unit file has a unique name (e.g., nginx.service) and is stored in /etc/systemd/system/ or /lib/systemd/system/.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text:
• [Unit]: Metadata and dependencies (e.g., Description, After, Requires).
  • [Service]: Process control (e.g., ExecStart, Restart, User).
  • [Install]: Installation directives (e.g., WantedBy, Alias).
  • [Scope] or [Slice]: For managing resource limits or grouping units.

docs.title: Example: Basic Service Unit File
docs.text:
[Unit]
Description=Example Service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/example-service
Restart=always
User=example-user
Group=example-group

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Syntax Rules
docs.text:
• Keys are case-sensitive (e.g., User vs. user).
  • Values must be quoted if they contain spaces.
  • Use [Unit] for dependencies and [Service] for process control.

docs.title: Best Practices for Maintainability
docs.text:
1. Use Descriptive Names and Comments Avoid ambiguous names like service1. Use nginx.service for clarity. Add inline comments (e.g., # Ensure network is up before starting).

  2. Avoid Redundant Dependencies Use Requires and After to enforce ordering, but avoid over-specifying. For example, After=network.target ensures the service starts after the network is ready.

  3. Leverage Systemd Features Replace custom scripts with systemd-native features like:

  4. Sockets for listening on ports (example.socket).
  5. Timers for periodic tasks (example.timer).

  6. Mount Units for automounting filesystems.

  7. Use Environment Files Store configuration variables in /etc/default/ or /etc/systemd/system/example.service.d/override.conf using EnvironmentFile.

  8. Minimize ExecStart Complexity Avoid chaining commands in ExecStart. Use separate units or scripts for complex logic.

docs.title: Security and Resource Management
docs.text:
1. Drop Privileges Set User and Group to non-root accounts. Use PrivateTmp=true to isolate temporary files.

  2. Restrict Capabilities Use AmbientCapabilities= to limit privileges (e.g., AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE).

  3. Enable Protection Features Add ProtectSystem=strict to prevent file system modifications. Use ProtectHome=true to block access to user home directories.

  4. Set Resource Limits Control memory and CPU usage with: 

    LimitCPU=50
LimitMEM=512M
    Adjust values based on system requirements.

  5. Use Secure Defaults Enable PrivateDevices=true to isolate hardware devices and NoNewPrivileges=true to prevent privilege escalation.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls to Avoid
docs.text:
1. Forgetting to Reload After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload to apply changes.

  2. Using Absolute Paths Avoid hardcoding paths like /usr/bin/example-service. Use relative paths or environment variables.

  3. Misconfigured Restart Policies Restart=always ensures the service restarts on failure, but Restart=on-failure is often sufficient.

  4. Incorrect Dependencies Missing After or Requires can cause services to start in the wrong order, leading to failures.

  5. Not Testing Changes Use systemctl start example.service and journalctl -u example.service to debug issues.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use clear, descriptive names and comments for readability.
  • Leverage systemd-native features (sockets, timers) instead of custom scripts.
  • Prioritize security by dropping privileges and restricting capabilities.
  • Avoid redundancy in dependencies and use daemon-reload after edits.
  • Test changes with systemctl and journalctl to ensure reliability.

docs.title: Targets & Runlevels
docs.text: Systemd introduced the concept of targets as a modern replacement for the traditional init system's runlevels. While runlevels were numeric (0–6) and rigidly defined, systemd targets are named, hierarchical, and flexible, enabling more granular control over system states. This section explores how systemd targets function, how they differ from legacy runlevels, and their role in managing system behavior.

docs.title: Understanding Systemd Targets
docs.text:
Systemd targets are analogous to runlevels but offer greater flexibility. Each target represents a predefined set of services and dependencies that define a system state. Common targets include:

  • multi-user.target (equivalent to runlevel 3): Minimal multi-user mode without a graphical interface.
  • graphical.target (equivalent to runlevel 5): Full graphical desktop environment.
  • rescue.target: A minimal state for troubleshooting, similar to runlevel 1.
  • emergency.target: A bare-bones state for critical recovery, akin to runlevel 0.

Unlike runlevels, targets can have dependencies on other units (e.g., services, sockets), allowing systemd to automatically enable or disable services when switching states. This ensures consistency and reduces manual configuration.

docs.title: Traditional Runlevels vs. Systemd Targets
docs.text:
Feature Traditional Runlevels (init) Systemd Targets Representation Numeric (0–6) Human-readable names State Definition Static, predefined Dynamic, with dependencies Service Management Manual switching (e.g., telinit 3) Automated via systemctl isolate Default State /etc/inittab defines default systemctl get-default determines Customization Limited Fully customizable

For example, switching to runlevel 3 in init required executing telinit 3, while systemd uses systemctl isolate multi-user.target to achieve the same result. The latter approach ensures services are properly enabled or disabled based on the target's dependencies.

docs.title: Switching Between Targets
docs.text:
Use systemctl isolate <target> to transition the system to a specific target. For example: 

sudo systemctl isolate graphical.target
This starts the graphical interface and stops services not required for that state.

docs.title: Checking the Default Target
docs.text:
systemctl get-default
Output might show graphical.target or multi-user.target, depending on the system's configuration.

docs.title: Setting a New Default Target
docs.text:
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
This changes the system's default boot state to multi-user mode.

docs.title: Listing Available Targets
docs.text:
systemctl list-units --type=target
This displays all predefined targets and their current status.

docs.title: Custom Targets and Use Cases
docs.text:
Systemd allows creating custom targets for specialized scenarios. For instance, a maintenance target could be defined to disable non-essential services: 

sudo systemctl enable maintenance.target
sudo systemctl isolate maintenance.target
Custom targets are useful for temporary states like backup operations or security audits.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Targets replace runlevels: They offer descriptive names and dynamic dependency management.
  • Automation: Switching targets automatically enables/disables services based on dependencies.
  • Flexibility: Custom targets enable tailored system states for specific use cases.
  • Commands: Use systemctl isolate, get-default, and set-default to manage targets.
  • Modern approach: Targets simplify system state transitions compared to the rigid, numeric runlevel model.

docs.title: Multi-User Envs
docs.text: Systemd replaces traditional init system runlevels with targets, which are abstract groupings of services. While runlevels (e.g., runlevel 3) were used in SysV init, systemd uses targets like multi-user.target (server-focused) and graphical.target (desktop environment). Managing these targets allows administrators to control service states and environment configurations effectively.

docs.title: Switching Between Targets
docs.text: To switch between targets, use systemctl isolate [TARGET]. This command stops all services from the previous target and starts those defined in the new target.

docs.title: Example: Switch to Multi-User Target
docs.text:
sudo systemctl isolate multi-user.target
This is equivalent to booting into a server environment without a graphical interface.

docs.title: Example: Switch to Graphical Target
docs.text:
sudo systemctl isolate graphical.target
This activates a desktop environment (e.g., GNOME, KDE) by starting services like gdm.service or lightdm.service.

docs.title: Check Current Default Target
docs.text:
systemctl get-default
Output might show multi-user.target (default for servers) or graphical.target (default for desktops).

docs.title: Set a New Default Target
docs.text:
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
This changes the default target for future boots. Use graphical.target for desktop environments.

docs.title: Configuring Multi-User Environments
docs.text: The multi-user.target is ideal for headless servers. However, you can customize it by enabling/disabling services:

docs.title: Enable a Service for Multi-User
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable nginx.service
This ensures nginx starts when multi-user.target is active.

docs.title: Disable a Service
docs.text:
sudo systemctl disable sshd.service
Prevents sshd from starting in multi-user mode.

docs.title: Verify Active Services
docs.text:
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=active
Filters services active in the current target.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Target Switches
docs.text:
• Service Conflicts: If a service fails to start after switching targets, check its dependencies: 
    systemctl status [SERVICE]
  • Target Not Found: Ensure the target exists (e.g., graphical.target requires a desktop environment like GNOME).
  • Persistent Changes: Use set-default to ensure the target persists across reboots.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use systemctl isolate to switch between targets, which control service states.
  • multi-user.target is optimal for servers, while graphical.target is for desktops.
  • Customize multi-user environments by enabling/disabling services.
  • Always verify target dependencies and use set-default for persistent configuration.

docs.title: journalctl Basics
docs.text: Systemd Journalctl Basics Systemd's journalctl is the primary utility for querying and managing logs generated by the journald service, which is the systemd component responsible for centralized logging. Unlike traditional syslog daemons, journald stores logs in a binary format, enabling efficient storage, structured data, and integration with systemd units. journalctl provides a powerful CLI interface to inspect, filter, and analyze these logs, making it essential for troubleshooting services, monitoring system events, and auditing system behavior.

docs.title: Basic Usage and Syntax
docs.text:
The core syntax for journalctl is: 

journalctl [OPTIONS...] [MATCHES...]
- --version: Display the version of journalctl. - -x: Expand log lines with explanations (useful for parsing structured data). - -b: Show logs from the current boot session. - --list-boots: List all boot sessions (useful for multi-boot logs).

Example: 

journalctl -x --since "1 hour ago"
This command retrieves logs from the last hour, expanding each line for clarity.

docs.title: Filtering Logs
docs.text:
journalctl allows precise filtering using unit names, priorities, keywords, and time ranges.

  • By Unit: 

    journalctl -u sshd.service
    Filters logs specific to the sshd.service unit.

  • By Priority: 

    journalctl -p 3
    Shows only error (level 3) logs. Priorities range from 0 (emerg) to 7 (debug).

  • By Time Range: 

    journalctl --since "2023-10-01 08:00:00" --until "2023-10-01 09:00:00"
    Restricts logs to a specific time window.

  • By Keywords: 

    journalctl _COMM=crond
    Filters logs from the crond process.

docs.title: Real-Time Monitoring
docs.text:
To monitor logs in real time: 

journalctl -f
This follows the log output, similar to tail -f, and is ideal for observing service startups, crashes, or ongoing processes.

For continuous monitoring of a specific unit: 

journalctl -u nginx.service -f

docs.title: Managing Journal Storage
docs.text:
journald can be configured to limit disk usage via /etc/systemd/journald.conf. Key options include: - SystemMaxUse: Maximum size of the journal (e.g., 100M). - SystemKeepFree: Minimum free disk space (e.g., 1G).

To apply changes: 

sudo systemctl restart journald.service

For manual log rotation or cleanup: 

sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=1d  # Delete logs older than 1 day
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=100M  # Delete logs until journal is 100M

docs.title: Troubleshooting Tips
docs.text:
• Missing Logs: Ensure journald is running (systemctl status journald).
  • No Pager: Use --no-pager to bypass the default pager for easier reading.
  • Large Logs: Use --output=json or --output=json-pretty for structured analysis.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• journalctl is the primary tool for interacting with systemd's journald logging system.
  • Logs are stored in a binary format, optimized for efficiency and structured data.
  • Use filters like -u, -p, --since, and --until to narrow down log searches.
  • Real-time monitoring with -f is invaluable for observing dynamic system behavior.
  • Configure journald to manage disk usage and automate log cleanup.

docs.title: Querying Logs
docs.text: The journalctl utility is the primary tool for querying and analyzing logs managed by the systemd journal. It allows administrators to filter, search, and inspect logs from services, kernel events, and user sessions. This section covers techniques for querying and filtering logs effectively.

docs.title: Basic Querying with journalctl
docs.text:
To retrieve logs, use journalctl with time-based filters or to follow real-time logs. Example: 

# Show logs from the last hour
journalctl --since "1 hour ago"

# Follow real-time logs (similar to 'tail -f')
journalctl -f

Use --until to limit logs to a specific time range: 

journalctl --since "2023-10-01 08:00:00" --until "2023-10-01 09:00:00"

docs.title: Filtering by Unit, Service, or Process
docs.text:
Filter logs for a specific systemd unit (e.g., a service or target): 

journalctl -u sshd.service

Filter by log level (e.g., error, warning): 

journalctl --level=err

Combine filters for precise results: 

# Show error logs for the apache2 service
journalctl -u apache2.service --level=err

docs.title: Advanced Filtering with journalctl Options
docs.text:
Use --grep to search for specific text in logs: 

journalctl --grep="Failed to bind"

For more complex patterns, use --grep with regular expressions: 

journalctl --grep="^Failed" --color

Filter by process ID (PID) or unit name using _PID or _SYSTEMD_UNIT: 

journalctl _PID=1234
journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=nginx.service

docs.title: Analyzing and Exporting Logs
docs.text:
Export logs to a file for analysis: 

journalctl -u sshd.service > sshd_logs.txt

Use --output=json to extract structured data: 

journalctl --output=json

For advanced analysis, pipe logs to tools like jq for JSON processing: 

journalctl --output=json-pretty | jq '.'

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use --since and --until to narrow logs to specific time ranges.
  • Filter by unit, service, or log level to focus on relevant entries.
  • Combine --grep and regular expressions for precise text matching.
  • Export logs to files or use JSON output for structured analysis.
  • Leverage --rotate and log rotation settings to manage storage efficiently.

docs.title: Timer Units
docs.text: Systemd timers provide a powerful mechanism for scheduling services to run at specific times or intervals, abstracting the complexity of traditional cron jobs. A timer unit is a special type of systemd unit that manages the execution of associated service units based on predefined schedules. Timers are defined in .timer files, which are linked to corresponding .service files. When a timer triggers, it activates the service unit, allowing for precise control over when tasks are executed.

docs.title: Key Components of a Timer Unit
docs.text:
A timer unit file (e.g., example.timer) contains a [Unit] section for metadata and a [Timer] section for scheduling logic. The core directive is OnCalendar, which specifies the schedule using a cron-like syntax. Additional directives like OnUnitActiveSec (delay after the unit becomes active) and OnUnitInactiveSec (delay after the unit becomes inactive) can refine timing behavior.

Example example.timer file: 

[Unit]
Description=Run daily backup

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
OnUnitActiveSec=15
Unit=example.service

  • OnCalendar=daily schedules the service to run once per day.
  • OnUnitActiveSec=15 adds a 15-second delay after the service becomes active.
  • Unit=example.service links the timer to the service unit.

docs.title: Relationship to Service Units
docs.text:
A timer unit acts as a scheduler for its associated service unit. When the timer triggers, it activates the service unit (e.g., starts, restarts, or reloads it). The service unit must be defined in a .service file, and the timer unit must explicitly reference it via the Unit= directive.

Dependencies: - The timer unit depends on the service unit being active. If the service unit is not properly configured, the timer may fail to trigger. - Timers can be configured to run one-time tasks or recurring schedules, depending on OnCalendar settings.

docs.title: 1. Daily Backup Task
docs.text:
A timer that runs a backup service every day at 2:00 AM: 

[Timer]
OnCalendar=0 2 * * *
Unit=backup.service

docs.title: 2. Weekly System Update
docs.text:
A timer that triggers a system update every Sunday at 10:00 PM: 

[Timer]
OnCalendar=0 22 * * Sun
Unit=update.service

docs.title: 3. One-Time Task
docs.text:
A timer that runs a script once at a specific time: 

[Timer]
OnCalendar=2024-05-15 14:30:00
Unit=one-time-task.service

docs.title: Managing Timers
docs.text:
Use systemctl to enable, start, or check timer status: 

# Enable the timer to persist across reboots
sudo systemctl enable example.timer

# Start the timer immediately
sudo systemctl start example.timer

# List all active timers
systemctl list-timers

The list-timers command shows details like the next scheduled run time and whether the timer is active.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Timer units schedule service units using OnCalendar and other timing directives.
  • Service units must be explicitly referenced in the timer file.
  • Commands like systemctl enable and list-timers are essential for managing and monitoring timers.
  • Timers abstract scheduling complexity, replacing or complementing traditional cron jobs.
  • Use cron-like syntax for OnCalendar to define daily, hourly, or custom schedules.

docs.title: Configuring Timers
docs.text: Systemd timers provide a powerful mechanism to schedule services to run at specific times or intervals. By combining .timer unit files with corresponding .service units, you can automate recurring tasks such as backups, system checks, or maintenance routines. This section demonstrates how to create, manage, and troubleshoot systemd timers.

docs.title: Understanding Timer Unit Files
docs.text:
A .timer unit file defines when a service should be triggered. It includes two main sections: - [Unit]: Describes the timer's purpose and dependencies. - [Timer]: Specifies scheduling rules, such as intervals or calendar-based triggers.

Example structure: 

[Unit]
Description=Daily System Check

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Unit=syscheck.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

Key timer options in the [Timer] section: - OnCalendar: Schedule based on dates/times (e.g., daily, * * * * * for cron-like syntax). - OnUnitActiveSec: Trigger after a service has been active for a duration. - OnBootSec: Trigger after a delay following system boot. - AccuracySec: Define how precisely the timer should align with the schedule.

docs.title: Creating a Timer
docs.text:
1. Define the service: Create a .service file for the task. For example, a script that logs system metrics: 

    [Unit]
Description=System Metrics Logger

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/log_metrics.sh
Type=oneshot

  2. Create the timer: Write a .timer file to schedule the service. To run the service every hour: 

    [Unit]
Description=Run System Metrics Logger Hourly

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*:*:*:0/1
Unit=sysmetrics.service
AccuracySec=1h

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

  3. Enable and start the timer: 

    sudo systemctl enable sysmetrics.timer
sudo systemctl start sysmetrics.timer

The AccuracySec option ensures the timer aligns with the specified interval, even if delayed.

docs.title: Managing Timers
docs.text:
Use systemctl to interact with timers: - List active timers: 

systemctl list-timers
Output includes the next scheduled run time and status.

  • Trigger a timer immediately: 

    sudo systemctl start sysmetrics.timer
    Use --now to force execution without waiting for the next scheduled time: 
    sudo systemctl --now start sysmetrics.timer

  • Modify a timer: Edit the .timer file and reload systemd: 

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart sysmetrics.timer

  • Disable or stop a timer: 

    sudo systemctl disable sysmetrics.timer
sudo systemctl stop sysmetrics.timer

docs.title: Troubleshooting Timers
docs.text:
Common issues and solutions: - Timer not triggering: Check logs with: 

journalctl -u sysmetrics.timer
Ensure the service unit (sysmetrics.service) exists and is valid. - Incorrect scheduling: Verify OnCalendar syntax matches systemd's format (e.g., * * * * * for every minute). - Permissions: Ensure the timer unit file is owned by root and has correct permissions (-rw-r--r--).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Timers link to services: A .timer unit must reference a valid .service unit.
  • Use OnCalendar for flexibility: Cron-like syntax enables precise scheduling.
  • Monitor with systemctl list-timers: Track active and pending timer events.
  • Debug with journalctl: Logs reveal errors in timer or service execution.

docs.title: I/O Resource Limits (with examples of CPU and memory limits)
docs.text:
BlockIO restricts disk I/O bandwidth for specific devices by specifying device paths and limits. The correct syntax is BlockIO=DEVICE:READ_BPS:WRITE_BPS, where DEVICE is the path to the block device (e.g., /dev/sda), and READ_BPS/WRITE_BPS define read/write byte-per-second limits. Major:minor notation is not valid for BlockIO. IOWeight (with updated syntax) is used for I/O prioritization. Modern systems use IOWeight=weight with explicit weight values (e.g., IOWeight=500) to prioritize I/O operations.

Example: 

[Service]
CPUQuota=50%
MemoryLimit=1G
BlockIO=/dev/sda:50M:10M
BlockIO=/dev/sdb:10M:50M
IOWeight=500
- CPUQuota=50% limits CPU usage to 50% of a single core. - MemoryLimit=1G restricts memory usage to 1 gigabyte. - BlockIO=DEVICE:READ_BPS:WRITE_BPS specifies the maximum read/write bandwidth for a device. - IOWeight=500 prioritizes I/O operations (higher values = lower priority).

Commands: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart <service-name>

docs.title: systemd-nspawn
docs.text: Systemd-nspawn is a lightweight containerization tool included in the systemd suite, designed to create sandboxed environments for running isolated processes or entire operating systems. Unlike full container runtimes like Docker, nspawn leverages systemd's built-in capabilities to manage namespaces, cgroups, and process isolation, making it ideal for testing, development, or running untrusted code in a controlled environment. It operates by booting a minimal root filesystem and launching a systemd instance within it, allowing for fine-grained control over resource allocation and process isolation.

docs.title: Setting Up a Container Environment
docs.text: To use nspawn, you first need a root filesystem for the container. This can be created using tools like debootstrap (for Debian/Ubuntu) or tar archives. Below is an example workflow using debootstrap:

docs.title: 1. Create a Directory for the Container
docs.text: mkdir -p /var/lib/mycontainer

docs.title: 2. Set Up the Root Filesystem
docs.text:
debootstrap --arch=amd64 bullseye /var/lib/mycontainer
This creates a minimal Debian Bullseye root filesystem in /var/lib/mycontainer.

docs.title: 3. Configure Systemd Units (Optional)
docs.text:
Create a systemd unit file (e.g., /etc/systemd/system/mycontainer.service) to define how the container should be started: 

[Unit]
Description=My Container

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/nspawn --bind=/etc/resolv.conf:/etc/resolv.conf --tmpfs /tmp --network=host /var/lib/mycontainer
Restart=always
This example binds the host's DNS configuration, mounts a tmpfs for /tmp, and uses host networking.

docs.title: Running and Managing Containers
docs.text: Once the environment is prepared, you can launch the container using systemd-nspawn:

docs.title: 1. Start the Container
docs.text:
systemctl start mycontainer
This starts the container as defined in the unit file. You can also launch it interactively: 
systemd-nspawn --bind=/etc/resolv.conf:/etc/resolv.conf --tmpfs /tmp --network=host /var/lib/mycontainer

docs.title: 2. Use Bind Mounts and tmpfs
docs.text:
Bind mounts allow sharing files between the host and container. For example: 

--bind=/home/user/data:/data
Mounts /home/user/data from the host to /data in the container. Use --tmpfs to create temporary filesystems in memory.

docs.title: 3. Networking Options
docs.text:
• --network=host: Share the host's network stack.
  • --network=bridge: Use a virtual bridge (default).
  • --network=none: Disable networking entirely.

docs.title: 1. Cgroups and Resource Limits
docs.text: Use --cpu=2 or --memory=1G to limit CPU and memory usage. These parameters are passed to the container's cgroups.

docs.title: 2. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Namespaces: nspawn isolates processes, IPC, and network stacks by default.
  • SELinux/AppArmor: Enable these to restrict container privileges further.
  • User Namespaces: Use --user to run the container as a non-root user.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Common Issues
docs.text:
• Missing Libraries: Ensure all required binaries are present in the container's root filesystem.
  • Permission Errors: Use --bind to grant access to host files or adjust ownership.
  • Logs: Check container logs with: 
    journalctl -u mycontainer

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• systemd-nspawn provides lightweight sandboxing by leveraging systemd's isolation features.
  • Containers require a root filesystem and can be configured with bind mounts, tmpfs, and networking options.
  • Use systemd units to manage container lifecycle and resource limits.
  • Security is enhanced through cgroups, namespaces, and SELinux/AppArmor integration.
  • Debug with journalctl and ensure all dependencies are present in the container's environment.

docs.title: Diagnosing Boot Failures with Systemd
docs.text: Boot failures in Linux systems often stem from systemd services failing to start during the initramfs or kernel boot process. Systemd provides robust tools to diagnose these issues, primarily through journal logs and service status checks. This section guides you through systematic troubleshooting steps to identify and resolve root causes.

docs.title: Accessing Journal Logs for Boot Analysis
docs.text:
The systemd journal is the primary source of information for boot failures. Use journalctl to inspect logs from the current or previous boot:

journalctl -b

This command displays logs from the last boot. To focus on critical errors, filter with --since and --until:

journalctl -b --since "07:00:00" --until "07:10:00"

Look for entries with ERR, CRIT, or PANIC severity. For example, a failed service might show:

Failed to start Network Manager: Unit network-manager.service not found.

docs.title: Checking Service Status and Dependencies
docs.text:
If a service fails to start, use systemctl to investigate its status:

systemctl list-units --state=failed

This lists all failed units. For detailed diagnostics, check the status of a specific service:

systemctl status <service-name>

For example, a failed networking service might reveal:

Failed with result 'exit-code'. See system journal for details.

Use journalctl again with the service name to drill down:

journalctl -u <service-name>

docs.title: Analyzing Unit Files and Dependencies
docs.text:
Corrupted or misconfigured unit files can cause boot failures. Inspect a service's unit file with:

systemctl cat <service-name>

Check for syntax errors, incorrect paths, or missing dependencies. For example, a typo in a ExecStart path might prevent the service from launching.

Verify dependencies using systemctl:

systemctl list-dependencies <service-name>

Ensure all required services are enabled and configured correctly.

docs.title: Checking Kernel and Initramfs Messages
docs.text:
Some boot failures originate from the kernel or initramfs. Use dmesg to inspect kernel ring buffer messages:
