    [DscProperty(Mandatory)]  
    [string]$Path  

    [DscProperty(Mandatory)]  
    [string]$Content  

    [DscProperty()]  
    [System.String]$Ensure = "Present"  

    [void] Get-TargetResource() {  
        $currentContent = Get-Content -Path $Path -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue  
        return @{"Path" = $Path; "Content" = $currentContent; "Ensure" = $Ensure}  
    }  

    [void] Set-TargetResource() {  
        if ($Ensure -eq "Present") {  
            if (-not (Test-Path -Path $Path)) {  
                New-Item -Path $Path -ItemType File | Out-Null  
            }  
            Set-Content -Path $Path -Value $Content  
        } else {  
            if (Test-Path -Path $Path) {  
                Remove-Item -Path $Path -Force  
            }  
        }  
    }  

    [bool] Test-TargetResource() {  
        $currentContent = Get-Content -Path $Path -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue  
        return ($currentContent -join "`n") -eq $Content -and (Test-Path -Path $Path)  
    }  
}

Use the resource in a configuration: 

Configuration FileConfig {  
    Node localhost {  
        FileContentResource MyFile {  
            Path = "C:\Test\myfile.txt"  
            Content = "This is the desired content."  
            Ensure = "Present"  
        }  
    }  
}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use DSCResourceSchema for parameter validation and documentation.
  • Handle errors gracefully to avoid partial configurations.
  • Ensure idempotency by avoiding destructive operations unless explicitly required.
  • Package resources as modules for reuse across environments.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Custom DSC resources extend DSC’s capabilities for specialized tasks.
  • Implement Get-TargetResource, Set-TargetResource, and Test-TargetResource methods.
  • Validate parameters with DSCResourceSchema and test thoroughly.
  • Structure resources for idempotency and reusability.
  • Package resources as PowerShell modules for deployment.

docs.title: Registering and Using Custom Resources
docs.text: Custom DSC resources extend the capabilities of Desired State Configuration (DSC) by enabling you to define reusable, modular logic for managing system resources. This section explains how to register custom resources with the DSC resource repository and apply them in configurations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before proceeding, ensure: - You have created a custom DSC resource (e.g., using New-DSCResource or manual development). - The resource is compiled into a module (e.g., MyCustomResource.psm1 and MyCustomResource.psd1). - The module is placed in a location accessible to the DSC runtime (e.g., C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules).

docs.title: Registering the Resource with the Repository
docs.text: To make your custom resource available to other systems or environments, register it with a DSC resource repository. This can be a local file system or a remote repository like the PowerShell Gallery.

docs.title: Local Registration
docs.text:
1. Place the module in the DSC module directory: 
    Copy-Item -Path "C:\Path\To\MyCustomResource.psm1" -Destination "C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules\MyCustomResource"
  2. Register the resource with the local repository: 
    Register-DSCResource -ModuleName "MyCustomResource"
    This command updates the local DSC resource repository to include your module.

docs.title: Remote Registration (PowerShell Gallery)
docs.text:
1. Publish the module to the PowerShell Gallery: 
    Publish-Module -Name "MyCustomResource" -Repository "PSGallery"
    Follow prompts to authenticate and upload the module.
  2. Install the module on target systems: 
    Install-Module -Name "MyCustomResource" -Repository "PSGallery" -Force

docs.title: Using the Custom Resource in Configurations
docs.text: Once registered, you can use the resource in DSC configurations.

docs.title: Example: Configuring a Custom Resource
docs.text:
Configuration MyCustomConfig {
    Node 'localhost' {
        MyCustomResource MyResource {
            Property1 = "Value1"
            Property2 = "Value2"
            Ensure = "Present"
        }
    }
}

# Compile and apply the configuration
MyCustomConfig
Start-DSCConfiguration -ConfigurationName MyCustomConfig -Wait -Verbose

Ensure the resource name matches the module name (e.g., MyCustomResource). Properties must align with the resource's defined schema.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Common Issues
docs.text:
• Resource Not Found: Verify the module is in the correct directory and registered. Use Get-DSCResource to list available resources.
  • Schema Mismatches: Check the resource's ResourceSchema.mof file for property definitions.
  • Permissions: Ensure the module directory has proper permissions for the DSC service account.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Register custom DSC resources with the local repository or PowerShell Gallery to share them across environments.
  • Use Register-DSCResource to update the DSC resource repository with your module.
  • Include custom resources in configurations by referencing their module name and properties.
  • Validate resource availability with Get-DSCResource and ensure schema alignment for successful execution.
  • Always test configurations in a non-production environment before deployment.

docs.title: Validating Custom DSC Resources with the DSC Testing Framework
docs.text: Testing custom DSC resources is critical to ensure they behave as expected in various scenarios. The DSC Testing Framework provides tools to validate resource functionality, simulate configurations, and debug issues. This section covers best practices for testing custom resources and troubleshooting common pitfalls.

docs.title: Setting Up the Testing Environment
docs.text:
Before testing, ensure the DscResourceTest module is installed. This module provides cmdlets for creating and running DSC tests. Run the following command to install it:

Install-Module -Name DscResourceTest -Force

Note: This module is available in PowerShell 5.1 and later. For Windows 10/21H2 or Windows Server 2019/2022, ensure the module is compatible with your PowerShell version.

docs.title: Writing Test Scripts
docs.text: A typical test script involves two steps: 1. Define a configuration that applies the custom resource. 2. Validate the state using Test-DscConfiguration or Invoke-DscResource.

docs.title: Example: Testing a Custom Service Resource
docs.text:
Assume a custom resource PS_DSCService manages Windows services. Here's a test script:

# Define a configuration that uses the custom resource
Configuration Test-PS_DSCService
{
    Node localhost
    {
        PS_DSCService MyService
        {
            Name = "MyCustomService"
            Ensure = "Present"
            State = "Running"
        }
    }
}

# Compile the configuration
Test-PS_DSCService -OutputPath .\TestConfig

# Test the desired state
$testResult = Test-DscConfiguration -ConfigurationPath .\TestConfig -Wait -Verbose

# Output results
if ($testResult.AllTestsPass) {
    Write-Host "Test passed: Resource meets the desired state."
} else {
    Write-Host "Test failed: Resource does not match the desired state."
}

Tip: Use -Wait to pause execution until the configuration completes, and -Verbose to capture detailed output.

docs.title: Debugging Common Issues
docs.text:
If tests fail, follow these steps to diagnose problems:

  1. Check DSC Logs: Review the Event Viewer under Windows Logs > Setup for DSC-related events (ID 41000-41010).

  2. Run with Debugging: Use Start-DscConfiguration with -Debug and -Wait to inspect intermediate states:

Start-DscConfiguration -ConfigurationPath .\TestConfig -Wait -Debug -Verbose
  1. Validate MOF Files: Ensure the generated .mof files are syntactically correct. Use Test-ResourceConfiguration to validate them:
Test-ResourceConfiguration -ConfigurationPath .\TestConfig
  1. Isolate Variables: Test edge cases (e.g., missing dependencies, invalid input) to identify resource-specific bugs.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Use the DscResourceTest module to automate testing of custom resources.
  • Structure test scripts with a configuration block and validation step.
  • Debug by inspecting DSC logs, using -Debug parameters, and validating MOF files.
  • Always test in a non-production environment to avoid unintended changes.
  • Validate edge cases to ensure robustness across different system states.

docs.title: Creating Composite Resources
docs.text: Composite resources in PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) allow you to encapsulate multiple DSC resources into a single reusable module. This approach promotes modularity, reusability, and simplifies complex configurations by abstracting individual components into logical units. Composite resources are particularly useful for scenarios requiring multiple interdependent resources, such as setting up a web server with IIS, a firewall rule, and a service.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Process
docs.text:
1. Define the Composite Resource Create a script file (e.g., MyCompositeResource.psm1) containing the composite resource definition. Use the Configuration keyword to define the resource and include the required DSC resources.

  2. Export the Composite Resource Use the Export-DscResource cmdlet to generate the .ps1xml file that defines the resource in the module. This step ensures the resource is recognized by DSC.

  3. Package into a Module Organize the resource files into a module directory structure with a .psd1 file to describe the module. This enables the composite resource to be imported and used like any other DSC resource.

docs.title: Example: Combining File and Registry Resources
docs.text:
# MyCompositeResource.psm1
Configuration FileAndRegistrySetup {
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$FilePath,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$RegistryKey
    )

    Import-DscResource -ModuleName PSDscResources

    File CreateFile {
        Ensure = 'Present'
        Type = 'File'
        DestinationPath = $FilePath
        Contents = 'This is a test file.'
    }

    Registry SetRegistryValue {
        Ensure = 'Present'
        Key = $RegistryKey
        ValueName = 'TestValue'
        ValueData = 'TestData'
        ValueType = 'String'
    }
}

docs.title: Exporting the Resource
docs.text:
Run the following command in a separate script or during module creation to export the resource:

Export-DscResource -ModulePath .\MyCompositeModule

docs.title: Using the Composite Resource
docs.text:
After packaging the module, you can use the composite resource in another configuration:

# MyConfiguration.ps1
Import-DscResource -ModuleName MyCompositeModule

Configuration WebServerSetup {
    Node localhost {
        FileAndRegistrySetup SetupWebServer {
            FilePath = 'C:\inetpub\testfile.txt'
            RegistryKey = 'HKLM:\Software\TestApp'
        }
    }
}

WebServerSetup -OutputPath .\ConfigOutput

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
• Module Structure: The composite resource must reside in a module directory with a valid .psd1 file.
  • Version Compatibility: Export-DscResource is available in PowerShell 5.1 and later.
  • Testing: Validate the composite resource in isolation before integrating it into larger configurations.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Composite resources bundle multiple DSC resources into a single reusable module.
  • Use Export-DscResource to generate the module definition file.
  • Structure modules with .psd1 and .psm1 files for proper recognition.
  • Composite resources simplify complex configurations by abstracting dependencies.
  • Always test composite resources in isolated environments before deployment.

docs.title: Using Composite Resources
docs.text: PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) composite resources allow you to encapsulate multiple DSC resources into a single reusable resource, simplifying complex configurations. By combining existing resources (e.g., File, Registry, or Service) into a custom resource, you can abstract logic, reduce redundancy, and improve maintainability. This section explains how to integrate composite resources into DSC configurations to manage multi-step deployments efficiently.

docs.title: Creating a Composite Resource
docs.text:
A composite resource is defined using the Configuration keyword and can include any valid DSC resource. For example, a WebServer composite resource might combine WindowsFeature, File, and Registry resources to configure IIS:

Configuration WebServerResource {
    param (
        [string]$WebsiteName = "DefaultWebSite",
        [string]$PhysicalPath = "C:\inetpub\wwwroot"
    )

    Import-DscResource -ModuleName PSDesiredStateConfiguration

    Node localhost {
        WindowsFeature IIS {
            Name = "Web-Server"
            Ensure = "Present"
        }

        File WebsiteContent {
            DestinationPath = $PhysicalPath
            Contents = "<html><body><h1>$WebsiteName</h1></body></html>"
            Ensure = "Present"
        }

        Registry WebsiteRegistry {
            Key = "HKLM:\Software\MyWebServer"
            ValueName = "SiteName"
            ValueData = $WebsiteName
            Ensure = "Present"
        }
    }
}

This resource ensures IIS is installed, creates a basic HTML file, and sets a registry value. The parameters (WebsiteName, PhysicalPath) allow customization.

docs.title: Using Composite Resources in Configurations
docs.text:
To use a composite resource in a configuration, first compile it into a module or save it as a .ps1 file. Then, import it and call it like any other DSC resource. For example:

# Compile the composite resource
WebServerResource -WebsiteName "MyAppSite" -PhysicalPath "C:\AppContent" -OutputPath .\WebServerResource.mof

# Use the composite resource in another configuration
Configuration MyWebServerConfig {
    Import-DscResource -ModuleName WebServerResourceModule

    Node localhost {
        WebServerResource WebServer {
            WebsiteName = "MyAppSite"
            PhysicalPath = "C:\AppContent"
        }
    }
}

MyWebServerConfig -OutputPath .\MyWebServerConfig.mof

In this example, the WebServerResource is reused to configure a custom web server. The composite resource handles internal dependencies, reducing boilerplate code.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Encapsulate logic: Group related resources (e.g., installing software, configuring services, setting permissions) into a single resource.
  • Parameterize inputs: Use parameters to make the composite resource flexible and reusable across different environments.
  • Test thoroughly: Validate the composite resource in isolation before integrating it into larger configurations.
  • Version control: Track changes to composite resources to ensure compatibility with dependent configurations.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Composite resources simplify complex DSC configurations by bundling multiple resources into a single, reusable unit.
  • They improve maintainability by abstracting logic and reducing redundancy.
  • Parameters allow customization, making composite resources adaptable to different deployment scenarios.
  • Always test composite resources in isolation to ensure reliability in production environments.

docs.title: 1. Prioritize Modularity and Encapsulation
docs.text:
• Break down configurations into logical, reusable components. For example, a "WebServer" composite resource might combine WindowsFeature, File, and Script resources to install IIS, configure static files, and deploy a website.
  • Example: 
    Resource WebServer {
    param (
        [string]$DestinationPath = 'C:\inetpub\wwwroot\index.html',
        [string]$Content = '<h1>Hello from DSC!</h1>'
    )
    Node localhost {
        WindowsFeature IIS {
            Ensure = 'Present'
            Name = 'Web-Server'
        }
        File StaticContent {
            DestinationPath = $DestinationPath
            Contents = $Content
            Ensure = 'Present'
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Use Parameters for Customization
docs.text:
• Expose parameters to allow users to customize behavior without modifying the resource. For instance, a DatabaseServer composite might accept InstanceName and DataDirectory parameters and use them in its logic.
  • Example: 
    Resource DatabaseServer {
    param (
        [string]$InstanceName = 'MSSQLSERVER',
        [string]$DataDirectory = 'C:\MSSQL\Data'
    )
    Node localhost {
        WindowsFeature SQLServer {
            Ensure = 'Present'
            Name = 'SQL-Server'
        }
        Registry SQLConfig {
            Key = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Microsoft SQL Server\$InstanceName\Setup"
            ValueName = 'DataDirectory'
            ValueData = $DataDirectory
            Ensure = 'Present'
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Validate Input Parameters
docs.text: • Implement validation to prevent invalid configurations. Use ValidateScript or ValidateRegex to enforce constraints on parameters.

docs.title: 1. Implement Unit and Integration Tests
docs.text:
• Use Pester to test individual components and their interactions. For example, verify that a composite resource correctly installs IIS and creates the static content file.
  • Example Pester test: 
    Describe 'WebServer Resource' {
    It 'Installs IIS' {
        Mock Get-WindowsFeature { return @{'Web-Server' = @{Install = $true}} }
        WebServer
        Get-WindowsFeature 'Web-Server' | Should -HaveProperty Install -ValueExactly $true
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Leverage the DSC Resource Schema
docs.text: • Validate your composite resource against the DSC Resource Schema to ensure compliance with Microsoft standards.

docs.title: 3. Test for Idempotency
docs.text: • Ensure your composite resource can apply the desired state multiple times without errors. For example, the File resource should handle idempotent updates to the same file.

docs.title: 1. Version Control and Documentation
docs.text: • Store composite resources in a version-controlled repository (e.g., Git). Include documentation explaining the resource’s purpose, parameters, and usage scenarios.

docs.title: 2. Manage Dependencies Explicitly
docs.text: • Clearly document dependencies between resources. For example, a DatabaseServer composite might depend on SQLServer and FirewallRule resources.

docs.title: 3. Use Semantic Versioning
docs.text: • Follow semantic versioning (e.g., 1.0.0, 2.1.0) to track changes. Major version updates should include backward-compatible improvements, while minor versions may introduce new features.

docs.title: Versioning and Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
• Deprecate gracefully: When removing parameters or changing behavior, provide a migration path and deprecation notice.
  • Avoid breaking changes: Ensure updates maintain compatibility with existing configurations unless absolutely necessary.
  • Use Get-DscResource for validation: Verify that your composite resource is recognized by the DSC runtime.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Design for modularity to simplify maintenance and reuse.
  • Thoroughly test with Pester and the DSC Resource Schema.
  • Version control and documentation are critical for collaboration and troubleshooting.
  • Prioritize backward compatibility to avoid disrupting existing deployments.
  • Validate inputs and ensure idempotency for robust, reliable configurations.

docs.title: PowerShell Objects
docs.text: PowerShell is fundamentally an object-oriented automation framework. Unlike traditional command-line tools that output plain text, PowerShell commands (cmdlets) return objects that encapsulate data and methods. These objects form the backbone of PowerShell's pipeline, enabling dynamic, data-rich automation. Understanding how to work with PowerShell objects is essential for advanced scripting and administration tasks.

docs.title: What Are PowerShell Objects?
docs.text:
PowerShell objects are instances of .NET classes or custom objects created in memory. They carry both data (properties) and behavior (methods). For example, the Get-Process cmdlet returns objects representing running processes, each with properties like Name, CPU, and Handles, and methods like Kill().

$process = Get-Process -Name "notepad"
$process.Name
$process.CPU

docs.title: .NET Objects vs. PowerShell Custom Objects
docs.text: PowerShell leverages the .NET Framework's object model, but it also allows you to create custom objects for specific tasks. The distinction matters when accessing properties and methods.

docs.title: .NET Objects
docs.text:
These are instances of .NET classes (e.g., System.Diagnostics.Process). You access their properties and methods using dot notation or casting:

$process = Get-Process -Name "explorer"
$process.BasePriority  # Access a property
$process.Kill()        # Call a method

docs.title: PowerShell Custom Objects
docs.text:
These are created using New-Object or the [pscustomobject] type accelerator. They are lightweight and ideal for ad-hoc data structures:

$customObj = [pscustomobject]@{
    Name = "Example"
    Value = 42
}
$customObj.Name

docs.title: Accessing Properties and Methods
docs.text: PowerShell provides multiple ways to interact with object properties and methods:

docs.title: 1. Dot Notation
docs.text:
$process = Get-Process -Name "cmd"
$process.Id

docs.title: 2. Select-Object for Property Filtering
docs.text: Get-Process | Select-Object -Property Name, CPU, WorkingSet

docs.title: 3. Get-Member to Discover Properties/Methods
docs.text: Get-Process | Get-Member

docs.title: The Pipeline and Object Flow
docs.text:
The PowerShell pipeline passes objects between cmdlets, enabling chained operations. Each cmdlet outputs objects that the next cmdlet processes:

Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 10 } | Sort-Object -Property CPU
  • Get-Process outputs process objects.
  • Where-Object filters objects based on their properties.
  • Sort-Object sorts objects by a property.

This flow allows complex logic without intermediate variables.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• PowerShell objects combine data and methods, enabling rich automation.
  • .NET objects are pre-defined classes, while custom objects are user-created for flexibility.
  • Use dot notation, Select-Object, or Get-Member to explore and manipulate objects.
  • The pipeline passes objects between cmdlets, enabling seamless, data-driven workflows.

docs.title: Pipeline Mastery
docs.text: PowerShell’s pipeline is a core mechanism for passing objects between cmdlets, enabling efficient data processing and automation. Unlike traditional text-based pipelines, PowerShell passes objects directly, allowing for rich, structured manipulation. Mastery of the pipeline involves understanding how to filter, sort, transform, and chain commands to automate complex tasks. This section explores advanced techniques for working with the pipeline in enterprise environments.

docs.title: Understanding the Pipeline
docs.text:
The pipeline passes objects from one cmdlet to the next, leveraging the $PSBoundParameters and $PSDefaultParameterValues for context. Each object in the pipeline is represented by the automatic variable $_, which holds the current object during processing.

Example: 

Get-Process | Select-Object -First 5
This command retrieves processes and selects the first five objects, demonstrating how objects are passed through the pipeline.

Key Concepts: - Object Flow: Cmdlets output objects (e.g., System.Diagnostics.Process), which are passed to subsequent cmdlets. - Pipeline Variable ($_): Represents the current object in the pipeline for script blocks.

docs.title: Filtering with Where-Object
docs.text:
Use Where-Object to filter objects based on properties or conditions. It accepts a script block to define the filtering logic.

Example: 

Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' }
This command lists only services with a status of "Running".

Advanced Filtering: 

Get-EventLog -LogName System | Where-Object { $_.EntryType -eq 'Error' -and $_.Source -like '*Service*' }
Filters error logs from specific sources.

Tip: Use -FilterParameter for simple property-based filtering (e.g., Where-Object { $_.Name -like 'SQL*' }).

docs.title: Sorting with Sort-Object
docs.text:
Sort-Object sorts objects by one or more properties. Use -Property to specify the sorting criteria and -Descending for reverse order.

Example: 

Get-Process | Sort-Object -Property CPU -Descending
Sorts processes by CPU usage in descending order.

Multiple Properties: 

Get-Service | Sort-Object -Property DisplayName, Status
Sorts services first by display name, then by status.

Note: Sort-Object returns a new sorted list; it does not modify the original data.

docs.title: Transforming with ForEach-Object
docs.text:
ForEach-Object processes each object in the pipeline, enabling custom transformations, calculations, or formatting.

Example: 

Get-Process | ForEach-Object { $_.Name + ' - ' + $_.CPU.ToString() }
Appends CPU usage to each process name.

Advanced Transformation: 

Get-Service | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        Name     = $_.Name
        Status   = $_.Status
        Started  = $_.StartTime
    }
}
Creates custom objects with selected properties.

Use Case: Combine with Where-Object for conditional transformations: 

Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' } | ForEach-Object { $_.Name }

docs.title: Advanced Techniques
docs.text:
1. Chaining Cmdlets: 

    Get-EventLog -LogName Application | Where-Object { $_.EntryType -eq 'Error' } | Sort-Object -Property TimeGenerated -Descending
    Filters, sorts, and processes event logs.

  2. Pipeline Variables in Scripts: Use $_ in script blocks to access objects during processing.

  3. Error Handling: Use try/catch blocks or Write-Error to manage pipeline errors gracefully.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• The pipeline passes objects between cmdlets, enabling structured data manipulation.
  • Where-Object filters objects based on dynamic conditions.
  • Sort-Object organizes data by properties, supporting multiple criteria.
  • ForEach-Object transforms objects, allowing custom calculations and formatting.
  • Advanced chaining and error handling enhance pipeline robustness in enterprise automation.

docs.title: Scripting Pipeline
docs.text: PowerShell’s pipeline is a powerful mechanism for passing objects between commands, enabling complex automation workflows. When building scripts, understanding how the pipeline operates, how to chain commands effectively, and how to handle errors is critical for reliability and performance. This section explores advanced techniques for working with the pipeline in scripts, including best practices for efficiency and robustness.

docs.title: Understanding Pipeline Flow in Scripts
docs.text:
The pipeline passes objects from one command to the next, allowing for seamless data transformation. In scripts, this flow is often used to process large datasets or filter results dynamically. For example: 

Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' } | Stop-Service
Here, Get-Service retrieves services, Where-Object filters running services, and Stop-Service terminates them.

Key Concepts: - Object piping: Commands output objects, not text. - Pipeline stages: Each stage processes objects sequentially. - Pipeline variables: Use $PSBoundParameters or $MyInvocation to access script parameters within the pipeline.

docs.title: Chaining Commands for Complex Logic
docs.text:
When building complex scripts, chain commands using the pipeline to avoid unnecessary data duplication. For instance: 

Get-EventLog -LogName System | Where-Object { $_.EntryType -eq 'Error' } | 
  Select-Object -Property TimeGenerated, Message | 
  Export-Csv -Path 'C:\Logs\Errors.csv' -NoTypeInformation
This script filters error logs, extracts relevant fields, and exports them to a CSV file.

Best Practice: - Use ForEach-Object for custom processing when the pipeline alone isn’t sufficient. - Avoid overloading the pipeline with excessive commands; break logic into modular functions if needed.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
The pipeline can become inefficient if not used judiciously. Here are key optimizations: 1. Limit data early: Filter results before processing to reduce memory and CPU usage. 

Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Data | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } | 
  Measure-Object -Property Length
2. Use -Parallel for scalability: In PowerShell 7.2+, ForEach-Object -Parallel can parallelize pipeline operations. 
1..100 | ForEach-Object -Parallel { Start-Sleep -Seconds 1; $_ } | 
  Measure-Command
3. Avoid unnecessary cmdlets: Replace Select-Object with calculated properties for performance.

docs.title: Error Handling and Pipeline Resilience
docs.text:
Errors in the pipeline can halt execution unless handled explicitly. Use try/catch blocks or -ErrorAction to control behavior: 

try {
    Get-Service -Name 'NonExistentService' | Stop-Service
} catch {
    Write-Warning "Failed to stop service: $_"
}
Pipeline-Specific Tips: - Use -ErrorAction Continue to allow the pipeline to proceed after an error: 
Get-Service | ForEach-Object { 
  try { Stop-Service -Name $_.Name } 
  catch { Write-Warning "Failed to stop $_.Name" } 
}
- Validate input objects before processing to prevent null reference errors.

docs.title: Best Practices for Scripting with the Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Prioritize filtering early: Reduce the dataset before expensive operations.
  2. Use ForEach-Object for custom logic: Avoid relying solely on the pipeline for complex transformations.
  3. Leverage pipeline variables: Access script parameters or context using $PSBoundParameters or $MyInvocation.
  4. Monitor resource usage: Use Measure-Command or Get-Process to track performance impacts.
  5. Document assumptions: Clearly define how objects are passed between stages to ensure maintainability.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• The pipeline enables efficient object-based processing but requires careful design for complex scripts.
  • Filter and limit data early to optimize performance and reduce resource consumption.
  • Use try/catch and -ErrorAction to handle errors gracefully and prevent script termination.
  • Combine the pipeline with ForEach-Object and modular functions for scalable, maintainable automation.
  • Always validate input objects and document assumptions to ensure robust script behavior.

docs.title: Module Structure
docs.text: PowerShell modules are foundational for reusable, maintainable automation in enterprise environments. A well-structured module ensures clarity, security, and compatibility across systems. This section outlines the core components of a PowerShell module, best practices for organization, and strategies for enterprise-grade development.

docs.title: 1. Module Manifest (*.psd1)
docs.text:
The manifest file defines metadata and exports for the module. It must reside in the module's root directory and use the .psd1 extension. Key properties include: - RootModule: Specifies the primary module file (e.g., MyModule.psm1). - ModuleVersion: Follow semantic versioning (e.g., 1.0.0). - GUID: A unique identifier for the module (generate using New-Guid). - FunctionsToExport/CmdletsToExport: Explicitly define what is exposed.

Example manifest snippet: 

@{
    RootModule = 'MyModule.psm1'
    ModuleVersion = '1.0.0'
    GUID = 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-g1h2-i3j4k5l6m7n8'
    FunctionsToExport = 'Get-Data', 'Set-Config'
    CmdletsToExport = ''
    NestedModules = 'NestedModule.psm1'
}

docs.title: 2. Module File (*.psm1)
docs.text:
Contains the actual PowerShell code (functions, cmdlets, variables). This file is loaded when the module is imported. Example: 

function Get-Data {
    return "Hello, World!"
}

function Set-Config {
    param ([string]$Path)
    Set-Item -Path $Path -Value "Enabled"
}

docs.title: 3. Exports
docs.text:
Use Export-ModuleMember to control what is available to users. Explicit exports prevent accidental exposure of internal functions: 

Export-ModuleMember -Function Get-Data, Set-Config

docs.title: Folder Structure for Enterprise Use
docs.text:
Organize modules into a structured directory to support scalability and collaboration: 

MyModule/
├── MyModule.psm1          # Main module code
├── MyModule.psd1          # Manifest file
├── src/                   # Source code (optional)
├── tests/                 # Unit tests (e.g., Pester scripts)
├── examples/              # Usage examples
├── README.md              # Documentation
└── bin/                   # Compiled binaries (if applicable)

  • src/: For organizing functions into submodules or categories.
  • tests/: Include Pester tests for validation.
  • examples/: Provide real-world usage scenarios.
  • README.md: Document installation, usage, and dependencies.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Semantic Versioning Use Major.Minor.Patch format for ModuleVersion to track changes and ensure backward compatibility.

  2. Unique GUID Generate a GUID for each module to avoid conflicts.

  3. Compatibility Specify $PSVersionTable requirements in the manifest to ensure compatibility with target environments.

  4. Security Sign modules with a certificate and restrict exports to minimize attack surfaces.

  5. Testing Integrate automated testing (e.g., Pester) and CI/CD pipelines for validation.

  6. Documentation Maintain clear, up-to-date documentation in README.md and examples.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Structure: Always include a .psd1 manifest and .psm1 code file.
  • Exports: Use Export-ModuleMember to control visibility.
  • Organization: Use subdirectories (src, tests, etc.) for scalability.
  • Security: Sign modules and limit exposed functions.
  • Versioning: Adopt semantic versioning for clarity and compatibility.

docs.title: Cmdlets & Functions
docs.text: PowerShell cmdlets and functions are the building blocks of automation, enabling you to encapsulate logic, enforce validation, and provide clear documentation for reusable code. This section guides you through creating custom cmdlets and functions, with a focus on parameter validation and help documentation to ensure robust and maintainable scripts.

docs.title: Creating Custom Cmdlets
docs.text:
Cmdlets are reusable PowerShell components that perform specific tasks. While creating cmdlets typically involves the Windows SDK and C#, you can also define cmdlet-like behavior using PowerShell functions with attributes. For advanced cmdlet development, use the New-Module cmdlet and a module manifest (*.psd1) to register cmdlets. For example:

# Example: Module manifest (MyModule.psd1)
@{
    RootModule = 'MyModule.psm1'
    CmdletsToExport = 'Get-ServiceStatus'
    FunctionsToExport = 'Test-PortAvailability'
    Guid = 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-g1h2-i3j4k5l6m7n8'
}

For simpler scenarios, use PowerShell functions with attributes to mimic cmdlet behavior.

docs.title: Creating Custom Functions
docs.text:
Functions are the primary way to create reusable logic in PowerShell. Define them using the function keyword. Here's a basic example:

function Get-ServiceStatus {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param (
        [string]$ServiceName
    )
    $service = Get-Service -Name $ServiceName -ErrorAction Stop
    return [PSCustomObject]@{
        Name     = $service.Name
        Status   = $service.Status
        Started  = $service.Started
    }
}

docs.title: Key Elements:
docs.text:
• [CmdletBinding()]: Enables advanced features like error handling and parameter validation.
  • param(): Defines input parameters.
  • [PSCustomObject]: Returns structured data.

docs.title: Parameter Validation
docs.text: Validate inputs to prevent errors and ensure correctness. Use the Validate attributes or custom validation logic:

docs.title: Built-in Validation Attributes
docs.text:
param (
    [ValidateScript({ $_ -ge 1 -and $_ -le 65535 })]
    [int]$Port
)

docs.title: Custom Validation Function
docs.text:
function Test-ValidPort {
    param ([int]$Port)
    return $Port -ge 1 -and $Port -le 65535
}

param (
    [ValidateScript({ Test-ValidPort $_ })]
    [int]$Port
)

For complex validation, use ValidateCount, ValidateRange, or ValidatePattern.

docs.title: Help Documentation
docs.text:
Add clear documentation using comment-based help (.SYNOPSIS, .DESCRIPTION, etc.):

<#
.SYNOPSIS
Checks if a service is running.
.DESCRIPTION
Retrieves the status of a Windows service and returns a custom object.
.PARAMETER ServiceName
The name of the service to check.
.EXAMPLE
Get-ServiceStatus -ServiceName "Spooler"
#>
function Get-ServiceStatus {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param (
        [string]$ServiceName
    )
    # Function implementation
}

Use Get-Help to view the documentation: 

Get-Help Get-ServiceStatus -Full

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use functions for simple, reusable logic and cmdlets for advanced, registered modules.
  • Validate parameters with attributes or custom functions to ensure robustness.
  • Document functions with comment-based help for clarity and usability.
  • Combine advanced features like error handling and structured output for professional-grade automation.

docs.title: Publishing Modules
docs.text: PowerShell modules are reusable packages that encapsulate cmdlets, functions, and scripts. Publishing them to the PowerShell Gallery makes them accessible to other administrators, while consuming modules allows you to leverage shared functionality in your automation workflows. This section covers the process of publishing and consuming custom PowerShell modules.

docs.title: Registering a PowerShell Gallery Account
docs.text:
Before publishing, you must create a free account on PowerShell Gallery. Use the Register-PSRepository cmdlet to associate your account with your local PowerShell environment: 

Register-PSRepository -Name "PSGallery" -Publisher "your_publisher" -DefaultRepository
This cmdlet prompts for your gallery credentials and stores them securely.

docs.title: Preparing Your Module
docs.text:
A module must include a module.psd1 file (the module manifest) and any supporting scripts. Ensure the manifest includes metadata like ModuleVersion, Description, and Author. For example: 

@{
    ModuleVersion = '1.0.0'
    Description = 'Custom module for system diagnostics'
    Author = 'Your Name'
    PowerShellVersion = '7.2'
    FunctionsToExport = @('Get-SystemHealth')
}
Organize your module files in a directory structure like: 
MyModule/
├── MyModule.psd1
└── Scripts/
    └── Get-SystemHealth.ps1

docs.title: Publishing the Module
docs.text:
Use Publish-Module to upload your module to the gallery: 

Publish-Module -Path "C:\MyModule\" -Repository "PSGallery"
- The module is validated for syntax, metadata, and dependencies before publication. - Ensure credentials are stored via Register-PSRepository instead of using -NuGetApiKey.

Note: The PowerShell Gallery enforces strict validation rules. Ensure your module adheres to gallery guidelines to avoid rejection.

docs.title: Installing Modules
docs.text:
Use Install-Module to download and install a module from the gallery: 

Install-Module -Name "MyModule" -Scope CurrentUser
- The -Scope parameter determines installation location: CurrentUser (default) or AllUsers. - For organizational use, install with -Scope AllUsers and ensure the module path is in your PSModulePath environment variable.

docs.title: Importing Modules into a Session
docs.text:
After installation, import the module into your current session: 

Import-Module -Name "MyModule"
This makes its cmdlets available for use. Verify with: 
Get-Command -Module "MyModule"

docs.title: Using Modules in Scripts
docs.text:
Modules can be imported in scripts using Import-Module at the top of the script. For example: 

# MyScript.ps1
Import-Module "MyModule"
Get-SystemHealth | Export-Csv "C:\Reports\health.csv"
Ensure the script has the correct execution policy (e.g., Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Publishing: Use Register-PSRepository and Publish-Module to share modules. Validate metadata and dependencies before submission.
  • Consuming: Install modules with Install-Module and import them into sessions or scripts with Import-Module.
  • Best practices: Always test modules in isolated environments before publishing, and use versioning to manage updates.
  • Security: Use -Scope CurrentUser for personal modules and ensure scripts have the correct execution policy for remote-signed modules.

docs.title: Remoting Basics
docs.text: PowerShell remoting enables administrators to execute commands and run scripts on remote Windows systems, streamlining management tasks across distributed environments. This capability is built on the PowerShell Remoting Protocol (PSRP), which operates over WinRM (Windows Remote Management), a service that implements the WS-Management protocol. By leveraging WinRM, PowerShell remoting allows secure, cross-platform remote execution while maintaining compatibility with PowerShell’s native scripting capabilities.

docs.title: How PowerShell Remoting Works
docs.text:
PowerShell remoting relies on WinRM as the transport layer and PSRP as the communication protocol. Here’s a high-level overview of the process: 1. Client Request: The local PowerShell session initiates a remote command using Enter-PSSession or Invoke-Command. 2. WinRM Transport: The request is sent over HTTP/HTTPS to the target machine’s WinRM service. 3. Remote Execution: The target machine processes the command, executes it in a remote session, and returns the results. 4. Secure Communication: Authentication (e.g., Kerberos, NTLM, or certificate-based) and encryption (via HTTPS) ensure secure data exchange.

This model allows administrators to manage multiple systems simultaneously while maintaining the context of the original session.

docs.title: WinRM Configuration
docs.text: WinRM is the backbone of PowerShell remoting. Proper configuration ensures reliable and secure remote execution.

docs.title: Basic Configuration Tasks
docs.text:
• Start/Stop WinRM Service: 

    # Start the WinRM service
Start-Service WinRM

# Check service status
Get-Service WinRM

  • Configure Listeners: WinRM listeners define how remote connections are accepted. The default listener uses HTTP, but HTTPS is recommended for production environments. 

    # Quick setup (HTTP and HTTPS listeners)
Set-WSManQuickConfig -Force

# Verify listener configuration
Get-WSManInstance -Namespace "root/cimv2" -ResourceUri "http://schemas.microsoft.com/wbem/wsman/1/wsman.xsd"

  • Firewall Rules: Ensure the firewall allows WinRM traffic: 

    # Enable WinRM firewall rule
netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group="Windows Management" new enable

  • HTTPS Setup: For HTTPS, configure a certificate and bind it to the listener: 

    # Register a certificate (example using a self-signed cert)
$cert = New-SelfSignedCertificate -DnsName "localhost" -CertStoreLocation "cert:\LocalMachine\My"

# Create an HTTPS listener
Register-WSManInstance -Action "CreateListener" -ResourceUri "https://localhost:5986" -Property @{
    Transport = "https"
    CertificateThumbprint = $cert.Thumbprint
}

docs.title: Establishing Remote Sessions
docs.text: Once WinRM is configured, use Enter-PSSession or Invoke-Command to interact with remote systems.

docs.title: Using Enter-PSSession
docs.text:
This command creates an interactive remote session: 

# Connect to a remote machine (requires credentials)
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName "RemoteServer" -Credential (Get-Credential)

Note: The target machine must have WinRM enabled and the user must have remote access permissions.

docs.title: Using Invoke-Command
docs.text:
This cmdlet runs a script or command remotely without an interactive session: 

# Run a command on a remote machine
Invoke-Command -ComputerName "RemoteServer" -ScriptBlock {
    Get-Service -Name "WinRM" | Select-Object Status, Name
}

For advanced scenarios, pass credentials or use the -FilePath parameter to execute scripts: 

Invoke-Command -ComputerName "RemoteServer" -Credential (Get-Credential) -FilePath "C:\Scripts\CheckServices.ps1"

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• PowerShell remoting is powered by WinRM and the PSRP protocol, enabling secure remote execution.
  • WinRM configuration includes starting the service, setting up listeners (HTTP/HTTPS), and enabling firewall rules.
  • Use Enter-PSSession for interactive sessions and Invoke-Command for non-interactive remote tasks.
  • Always prioritize HTTPS for secure communication and validate certificate trust in production environments.

docs.title: Runspace Pooling for Efficient Remote Execution
docs.text: Runspace pooling is a PSRP feature that reuses runspaces across multiple remote commands, reducing overhead and improving performance. A runspace pool manages a collection of runspaces that can be shared among remote sessions or commands, enabling efficient resource utilization for distributed tasks. Note: Runspace pools are created and managed locally, not on remote systems. Remote commands leverage existing pools rather than creating new ones.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Runspace: An execution context for PowerShell commands.
  • Pool: A collection of runspaces that can be dynamically allocated and released.
  • Benefits: Reduces memory and CPU usage, especially for high-throughput tasks like bulk configuration changes.

docs.title: Example: Creating and Using a Runspace Pool (PSRP-Compatible)
docs.text:
# Create a runspace pool locally (not on the remote system)
$runspacePool = [runspacefactory]::CreateRunspacePool(2, 5)
$runspacePool.Open()

# Execute remote commands using the local runspace pool
$scriptBlock = {
    $powerShell = [powershell]::Create()
    $powerShell.RunspacePool = $runspacePool
    $powerShell.AddScript({ Get-Service -Name "WinRM" })
    $result = $powerShell.Invoke()
}
Invoke-Command -ComputerName Server01 -ScriptBlock $scriptBlock

# Clean up
$runspacePool.Close()

docs.title: Advanced Use Case: Parallel Remote Commands (PSRP-Compatible)
docs.text:
# Create a runspace pool locally (not on the remote system)
$runspacePool = [runspacefactory]::CreateRunspacePool(2, 5)
$runspacePool.Open()

# Define a script block for remote execution
$script = {
    Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -like "svchost" }
}

# Use the pool to execute commands on multiple servers
$targets = @("Server01", "Server02", "Server03")
$results = @()
foreach ($server in $targets) {
    $powerShell = [powershell]::Create()
    $powerShell.RunspacePool = $runspacePool
    $powerShell.AddScript($script)
    $powerShell.AddParameter("ComputerName", $server)
    $results += $powerShell.Invoke()
}

# Clean up
$runspacePool.Close()

docs.title: Remote Job Management with PSRP
docs.text: Remote job management allows you to execute commands asynchronously on remote systems and monitor their progress. This is particularly useful for long-running tasks or workflows that require minimal user interaction. PSRP enables asynchronous execution via Invoke-Command without relying on local job systems. Note: PSRP's job management is distinct from local job persistence mechanisms like Start-Job.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Jobs: Background processes that run independently of the parent session.
  • Asynchronous Execution: Commands can run without blocking the caller.
  • Job Persistence: Jobs are not persisted across sessions; they are transient.

docs.title: Example: Starting and Monitoring a Remote Job (PSRP-Compatible)
docs.text:
# Start a remote job using PSRP's asynchronous execution (no -AsJob)
$job = Invoke-Command -ComputerName Server01 -ScriptBlock {
    Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object -First 5
}

# Monitor job status (PSRP-specific tracking)
Get-Job -Name "RemoteSystemCheck"
Receive-Job -Job $job
Stop-Job -Job $job
Remove-Job -Job $job

docs.title: Advanced Use Case: Job Persistence and Event Handling (PSRP-Compatible)
docs.text:
# Register an event to trigger a remote job when a service starts (PSRP-specific)
$scriptBlock = {
    Register-ObjectEvent -InputObject (Get-Service -Name "WinRM") -EventName "Start" -Action {
        $job = Start-Job -Name "ServiceStarted" -ScriptBlock {
            Write-Output "Service 'WinRM' has started."
        }
        Write-Host "Job '$job.Name' started."
    }
}

# Execute the script block on a remote system
Invoke-Command -ComputerName Server01 -ScriptBlock $scriptBlock

# Later, retrieve and manage the job
Get-Job -Name "ServiceStarted"
Receive-Job -Job "ServiceStarted"
Remove-Job -Name "ServiceStarted"

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Runspace pooling optimizes resource usage by reusing runspaces across remote commands, improving scalability for high-throughput tasks.
  • Remote job management enables asynchronous execution of commands via Invoke-Command without local job persistence, allowing administrators to monitor and manage long-running processes across distributed systems.
  • PSRP's support for these advanced techniques ensures efficient, scalable automation in enterprise environments.

docs.title: Securing Remoting Sessions
docs.text: Implement robust encryption, authentication, and audit logging to protect remote session integrity and confidentiality.

docs.title: Encryption Requirements
docs.text:
Enforce strong encryption protocols to secure data in transit: - TLS 1.2+ Enforcement: 

# Enable TLS 1.2 and disable older protocols  
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
Ensure servers and clients use TLS 1.2 or higher and disable TLS 1.0/1.1. - HTTPS Usage: Configure remoting endpoints (e.g., IIS, PowerShell remoting) to use HTTPS with valid SSL/TLS certificates.

docs.title: Authentication Best Practices
docs.text:
Strengthen access control to prevent unauthorized session entry: - Certificate-Based Authentication: 

# Configure WinRM to require client certificates  
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WinRM\Client" -Name "EnableCredSSP" -Value 1  
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WinRM\Client" -Name "TrustedHosts" -Value "*"
Use client certificates for mutual TLS authentication and validate certificate chains. - Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Integrate MFA via Azure AD, Microsoft Authenticator, or third-party solutions for administrative remoting. - Session Timeouts: 
# Set idle session timeout to 15 minutes  
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WinRM\Service" -Name "IdleTimeoutSec" -Value 900
Enforce session termination after inactivity and disable Keep-Alive to prevent persistent connections.

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text: Enable detailed logging to track remote session activity and detect suspicious behavior.

docs.title: Enable WinRM Logging
docs.text:
Configure WinRM to log requests and responses: 

# Set log directory and level (0 = None, 4 = Full)  
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WinRM\Service" -Name "LogLevel" -Value 4  
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WinRM\Service" -Name "LogPath" -Value "C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\WinRM"
Ensure the log directory exists and has appropriate permissions.

docs.title: Monitor Logs
docs.text: Use Event Viewer to review security events: - Event ID 4104: Successful WinRM connection. - Event ID 4105: Failed authentication attempt. - Event ID 4106: Successful authentication. Regularly analyze logs for anomalies, such as repeated failed attempts or unexpected client IPs.

docs.title: Try/Catch/Finally Blocks
docs.text: PowerShell's try/catch/finally blocks allow you to handle exceptions explicitly. The try block contains code that might throw an error, catch handles specific exceptions, and finally executes cleanup code regardless of errors.

docs.title: Example: Handling File Operations
docs.text:
try {
    $content = Get-Content -Path "C:\temp\missingfile.txt"
    Write-Output "File content: $content"
} catch {
    Write-Error "Failed to read file: $_"
} finally {
    Write-Host "Cleanup complete."
}
  • The catch block captures errors (e.g., file not found) and provides the error message via $_.
  • The finally block ensures resources are released or logs are flushed, even if an exception occurs.

docs.title: Custom Error Objects
docs.text: PowerShell's built-in error handling is flexible, but you can create custom error objects for richer diagnostics. Use the throw keyword with a custom exception object to define structured error data.

docs.title: Example: Throwing a Custom Error
docs.text:
$errorMessage = "Invalid user credentials"
$customError = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]::new(
    [System.Management.Automation.PSException]::new($errorMessage),
    "InvalidCredentials",
    [System.Management.Automation.ErrorCategory]::InvalidArgument,
    "C:\scripts\auth.ps1"
)
throw $customError
  • The ErrorRecord class allows you to specify error messages, categories, and source locations.
  • Use -ErrorAction in cmdlets to control how errors are handled (e.g., Stop, Continue, SilentlyContinue).

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Exit codes are integers returned by commands to indicate success or failure. PowerShell uses $LASTEXITCODE to store the exit code of the last executed command. This is particularly useful for scripts running in non-interactive environments.

docs.title: Example: Checking Exit Codes
docs.text:
# Run an external command and capture exit code
certutil.exe -generateSelfSignedCert "C:\cert\test.cer" > $null 2>&1
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
    Write-Error "Command failed with exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
}
  • Exit codes are often used in conjunction with if statements or switch blocks to determine next steps.
  • Always validate exit codes after external commands (e.g., net.exe, certutil.exe).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use try/catch/finally blocks to handle exceptions and ensure cleanup.
  • Create custom error objects with [ErrorRecord] for detailed diagnostics.
  • Leverage exit codes ($LASTEXITCODE) for script reliability in non-interactive contexts.
  • Combine try/catch with -ErrorAction to control error propagation.
  • Always validate exit codes after external commands to avoid silent failures.

docs.title: Debugging Scripts
docs.text: PowerShell debugging is essential for ensuring scripts run reliably in enterprise environments. When automation scripts fail, debugging helps identify root causes, such as logic errors, incorrect variable values, or unexpected side effects. This section covers core debugging techniques, including breakpoints, script analysis, and the Debug cmdlets, to help you diagnose and resolve issues efficiently.

docs.title: Setting Breakpoints
docs.text: Breakpoints pause script execution at specific points, allowing you to inspect variables, step through code, and evaluate conditions. PowerShell provides two main ways to set breakpoints: 1. Using Set-PSBreakpoint: Targets specific commands, variables, or script lines. 2. Using the Debugger: Interactive mode for exploring script state.

docs.title: Example: Setting a Breakpoint on a Command
docs.text:
Set-PSBreakpoint -Command "Get-ADUser"
This pauses execution whenever Get-ADUser is called. Run the script, and the debugger will activate at that point.

docs.title: Example: Conditional Breakpoint
docs.text:
Set-PSBreakpoint -Variable "userCount" -Action { $userCount -gt 100 }
Pauses execution when the $userCount variable exceeds 100.

Tip: Use Get-PSBreakpoint to list active breakpoints and Remove-PSBreakpoint to delete them.

docs.title: Script Analysis with Test-ScriptAnalyzer
docs.text: The Test-ScriptAnalyzer cmdlet checks scripts for common issues, such as hard-coded credentials, inefficient logic, or security risks. It leverages predefined rules to highlight potential problems.

docs.title: Example: Analyzing a Script
docs.text:
Test-ScriptAnalyzer -Path "C:\Scripts\ProcessUsers.ps1"
This runs the analyzer and outputs warnings or errors. For example, it might flag: 
PSRule: PSUseApprovedParameterNames: Use approved parameter names instead of 'userList'.

Customizing Rules: To disable specific rules: 

Test-ScriptAnalyzer -Path "ProcessUsers.ps1" -ExcludeRule "PSUseApprovedParameterNames"

docs.title: Debugging with Debug Cmdlets
docs.text: PowerShell’s Debug cmdlets provide low-level control over the debugging session. Use them to inspect the call stack, evaluate expressions, and modify variables dynamically.

docs.title: Example: Starting a Debug Session
docs.text:
Start-Debug -ScriptBlock { Get-ADUser -Filter * }
This launches an interactive debugger session for the script block. Use Stop-Debug to exit.

docs.title: Example: Evaluating Variables in Debug Mode
docs.text:
Debug-Command -Expression { $user.Properties }
Evaluates the expression in the current context and displays results.

Key Cmdlets: - Get-Debug: Lists active debug sessions. - Stop-Debug: Ends a debug session. - Debug-Command: Executes a command in the debugger.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Breakpoints (Set-PSBreakpoint) pause execution at specific commands or variables for inspection.
  • Script analysis (Test-ScriptAnalyzer) identifies common issues like security risks or inefficient logic.
  • Debug cmdlets (Start-Debug, Debug-Command) enable dynamic exploration of script state during runtime.
  • Combine these techniques to isolate bugs, validate logic, and ensure scripts meet enterprise compliance standards.

docs.title: Structured Logging with PowerShell
docs.text: Enterprise scripts require consistent, machine-readable logging to enable centralized monitoring and troubleshooting. PowerShell provides built-in cmdlets like Write-EventLog for writing to Windows Event Logs, which is a system destination. Structured logging refers to the format (e.g., JSON or CSV) used to represent log data, not the destination. For structured logging, implement custom functions to generate formatted entries. Use the Level parameter to categorize events (Verbose, Warning, Error, etc.) and include timestamps, source, and contextual data.

docs.title: Example: Structured Log Entry
docs.text:
function Log-Message {
    param (
        [string]$Message,
        [string]$Level = 'Information',
        [string]$LogFilePath = "$env:TEMP\script.log",
        [string]$EventLogName = 'Application',
        [string]$EventLogSource = 'MyScript'
    )
    $timestamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'
    $logEntry = @{
        Timestamp = $timestamp
        Level = $Level
        Message = $Message
        Source = $EventLogSource
        ScriptName = $MyInvocation.MyCommand.Name
        LineNumber = $MyInvocation.ScriptLineNumber
    }
    $jsonLog = $logEntry | ConvertTo-Json
    Write-Output $jsonLog
    $json,Log | Out-File -FilePath $LogFilePath -Append
    Write-EventLog -LogName $EventLogName -Source $EventLogSource -EventId 1001 -Message $jsonLog
}

# Example usage
Log-Message -Message "Failed to connect to server" -Level Error

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use JSON or CSV formats for machine-parsable logs.
  • Include script name, function name, and line numbers in log entries.
  • Store logs in a centralized location (e.g., UNC path) for audit trails.
  • Avoid conflating structured logging formats with Windows Event Log destinations.

docs.title: Event Tracing with Transcripts
docs.text: PowerShell’s Start-Transcript and Stop-Transcript cmdlets capture real-time script execution, including commands, errors, and output. This is ideal for debugging and post-mortem analysis.

docs.title: Example: Script Execution Transcript
docs.text:
Start-Transcript -Path "C:\Logs\ScriptTranscript_$(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMddHHmm').log" -IncludeInvocationHeader
try {
    # Simulate a script
    Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Stopped' }
} catch {
    Log-Message -Message "Script failed: $_" -Level Error
} finally {
    Stop-Transcript
}

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use -IncludeInvocationHeader to capture command-line context.
  • Combine with structured logging for dual logging (transcript + formatted logs).

docs.title: Writing to Windows Event Logs
docs.text: Windows Event Logs provide a centralized repository for system and application events. PowerShell scripts can write to these logs using Write-EventLog and query them using Get-WinEvent.

docs.title: Example: Writing to Event Log
docs.text: Write-EventLog -LogName Application -Source "MyScript" -EventId 1001 -Message "Script completed successfully"

docs.title: Example: Querying Event Logs
docs.text: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; ProviderName='MyScript'; ID=1001}

docs.title: Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
• Event Viewer: Use for real-time monitoring.
  • PowerShell: Automate log analysis with Get-WinEvent and filtering.
  • Third-party tools: Integrate with Splunk, ELK Stack, or Azure Monitor for centralized logging.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use structured logging formats (JSON/CSV) for centralized monitoring.
  • Leverage Start-Transcript for detailed script execution tracking.
  • Write to Windows Event Logs for system-wide visibility and compliance.
  • Combine structured logging with real-time monitoring tools for proactive issue detection.
  • Always include contextual data (timestamp, source, severity) in log entries.

docs.title: WMI Fundamentals
docs.text: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is a core Windows management technology that provides a unified interface for accessing system information, monitoring hardware and software resources, and performing administrative tasks. While newer standards like the Common Information Model (CIM) have evolved, WMI remains widely used for legacy systems and integration with older tools. PowerShell provides robust capabilities to query WMI classes, but note that Get-WmiObject is deprecated in PowerShell 5.1+ and replaced by Get-CimInstance for modern workflows.

docs.title: WMI Architecture Overview
docs.text:
WMI operates through three primary components: 1. WMI Service: A Windows service (winmgmt) that acts as the central management infrastructure. 2. Repository: A database storing WMI classes (definitions) and instances (data). Classes like Win32_Process or Win32_Service are stored here. 3. Providers: Bridge WMI to underlying hardware or software. For example, the Win32_Process provider interacts with the Windows process manager.

WMI classes are organized in namespaces, with root\cimv2 being the most common namespace for system-related classes. CIM (Common Information Model) is the modern standard that underpins WMI, ensuring consistency across platforms.

docs.title: Querying WMI with PowerShell
docs.text: PowerShell’s Get-CimInstance cmdlet is the recommended tool for querying WMI data in modern workflows. It replaces Get-WmiObject in PowerShell 5.1+ and offers improved performance and CIM-based compatibility.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text: Get-CimInstance -ClassName <ClassName> -Namespace <Namespace>

docs.title: Example: Retrieving System Information
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_ComputerSystem -Namespace root\cimv2
This retrieves details about the local machine, such as CPU architecture, total physical memory, and system manufacturer.

docs.title: Example: Listing Running Processes
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Process -Namespace root\cimv2 | Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CPU
This filters processes by their process ID, name, and CPU usage.

docs.title: Example: Querying Services
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service -Namespace root\cimv2 | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode
This lists all services, their current state (e.g., Running), and startup configuration.

docs.title: Common WMI Classes
docs.text: Class Name Description Win32_Process Represents running processes. Win32_Service Describes system services. Win32_NetworkAdapter Provides details about network interfaces. Win32_LogicalDisk Contains information about disks and partitions. Win32_Battery Reports battery status on laptops.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Tips
docs.text:
• Permissions: Many WMI queries require elevated privileges. Run PowerShell as Administrator if you encounter access denied errors.
  • Firewall: Ensure the WMI firewall rule is enabled to allow remote WMI queries.
  • Namespace Errors: Verify the correct namespace (e.g., root\cimv2) and class name spelling.
  • Error Handling: Use -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue or try/catch blocks to handle exceptions gracefully.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• WMI provides a unified interface for managing Windows systems, with root\cimv2 as the default namespace.
  • Use Get-CimInstance to query WMI classes like Win32_Process or Win32_Service for system insights.
  • Always validate permissions and namespaces to avoid access errors.
  • WMI is foundational for legacy systems, though modern CIM-based approaches are increasingly preferred.
  • Combine WMI queries with PowerShell’s pipeline for filtering and processing data efficiently.

docs.title: CIM Integration
docs.text: PowerShell 5.1 introduced native support for the Common Information Model (CIM), a modern, standardized framework for managing IT infrastructure. While WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) has been the traditional tool for system management in Windows, CIM provides a more robust, cross-platform, and extensible approach. This section explores how CIM integrates with PowerShell 5.1+, its advantages over WMI, and practical examples of querying CIM data.

docs.title: Evolution from WMI to CIM
docs.text:
CIM is a superset of WMI, built on the DMTF (Distributed Management Task Force) standards. Key differences include: - Cross-platform support: CIM is designed for use across Windows, Linux, and macOS via PowerShell 7.0+ and DSC (Desired State Configuration). - Improved performance: CIM queries are faster and more efficient than WMI, especially for large datasets. - Consistent API: CIM provides a unified interface for querying hardware, software, and configuration data. - Modern architecture: CIM relies on the CIMOM (Common Information Model Object Manager) instead of the older WMI service.

PowerShell 5.1+ includes the Microsoft.PowerShell.CimAutomation module, enabling direct access to CIM providers without requiring external tools like wbemtest or wmic.

docs.title: CIM Cmdlets in PowerShell 5.1+
docs.text: PowerShell 5.1+ provides the following CIM cmdlets: - Get-CimInstance: Queries CIM classes (replaces Get-WmiObject). - Get-CimClass: Retrieves metadata about CIM classes. - Get-CimSession: Manages CIM sessions for remote queries. - Invoke-CimMethod: Executes CIM methods (e.g., rebooting a system).

docs.title: Example: Querying System Information
docs.text:
# Get basic system info using CIM
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Manufacturer, Model

docs.title: Example: Listing Available CIM Classes
docs.text:
# List all CIM classes in the root/cimv2 namespace
Get-CimClass -Namespace root/cimv2 | Select-Object Name, Caption

docs.title: Example: Filtering Results
docs.text:
# Find all running processes with "chrome" in the name
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -like "*chrome*" } | Select-Object ProcessId, Name

docs.title: Querying CIM Classes and Properties
docs.text: CIM classes are organized into namespaces (e.g., root/cimv2). To query specific properties: 1. Use Get-CimInstance with the -ClassName parameter. 2. Use Select-Object to format output.

docs.title: Example: Customizing Output
docs.text:
# Get disk drive information with specific properties
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DiskDrive | Select-Object Model, Size, MediaType

docs.title: Example: Using CIM Methods
docs.text:
# Reboot the local machine using a CIM method
Invoke-CimMethod -ClassName Win32_OperatingSystem -MethodName Reboot

docs.title: Troubleshooting CIM Queries
docs.text:
Common issues include: - CIM service not running: Ensure the CIM Service (WmiPrvSE) is active: 

Get-Service -Name "CIM Service" | Select-Object Name, Status
- Permissions: Run PowerShell as Administrator for certain queries. - Namespace errors: Specify the correct namespace with the -Namespace parameter: 
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/cimv2 -ClassName Win32_Process

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• CIM is the modern successor to WMI, offering cross-platform, efficient, and standardized management capabilities.
  • PowerShell 5.1+ includes native CIM cmdlets like Get-CimInstance and Invoke-CimMethod for querying and managing systems.
  • Always verify the CIM service status and use -Namespace to target the correct CIM repository.
  • Use Select-Object to customize output and Where-Object to filter results effectively.
  • For advanced scenarios, combine CIM with DSC or PowerShell 7.0+ for full cross-platform support.

docs.title: Advanced WMI/CIM Automation
docs.text: WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) and CIM (Common Information Model) provide powerful capabilities for system monitoring, inventory collection, and configuration management. While WMI is the legacy framework, CIM is the modern, standardized replacement. This section demonstrates advanced techniques for leveraging these technologies in PowerShell scripts, including performance monitoring, hardware/software inventory, and configuration automation.

docs.title: Monitoring System Performance with WMI/CIM
docs.text: WMI and CIM can retrieve real-time performance metrics from local or remote systems. Use Get-CimInstance (preferred) or Get-WmiObject for querying.

docs.title: Example: Monitor Disk Usage
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_LogicalDisk | Where-Object { $_.DriveType -eq 3 } | Select-Object DeviceID, FreeSpace, Size
This retrieves free space and total size for all local drives (excluding removable drives).

docs.title: Example: Track CPU Load
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win30_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_Processor | Where-Object { $_.Name -like "*_Total*" } | Select-Object Name, PercentProcessorTime
Queries CPU usage across all cores.

docs.title: Example: Monitor Service Status
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.State -eq "Running" -and $_.StartMode -eq "Automatic" } | Select-Object Name, DisplayName
Lists all automatically started services that are currently running.

docs.title: Inventory Collection: Hardware and Software
docs.text: WMI/CIM can gather detailed system inventory, including hardware, OS, and installed software.

docs.title: Example: System Hardware Inventory
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Manufacturer, Model, TotalPhysicalMemory, SystemType
Provides system model, memory, and architecture details.

docs.title: Example: Installed Software Inventory
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Product | Select-Object Name, Version, Publisher
Lists installed software (note: Win32_Product may not capture all applications, especially those installed via MSI).

docs.title: Example: Network Adapter Information
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration | Where-Object { $_.IPEnabled -eq $true } | Select-Object IPAddress, DNSDomain
Retrieves IP addresses and DNS settings for active network adapters.

docs.title: Configuration Management with CIM
docs.text: CIM enables programmatic control of system settings, such as services, registry keys, and user accounts.

docs.title: Example: Start a Stopped Service
docs.text:
$service = Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service -Filter "Name='wuauserv'"
if ($service.State -eq "Stopped") {
    $service.StartService()
    Write-Output "Service 'Windows Update' started."
}
Starts the Windows Update service if it’s stopped.

docs.title: Example: Modify Registry Settings
docs.text:
$registry = Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32.Registry -Filter "Key='HKLM:\Software\MyApp'"
if ($registry) {
    $registry.SetValue("Enabled", 1, "DWORD")
    Write-Output "Registry key updated."
}
Sets a registry value (requires admin privileges).

docs.title: Example: Create a User Account
docs.text:
$account = Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_UserAccount -Filter "Name='NewUser'"
if (-not $account) {
    $newAccount = New-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_UserAccount -Property @{
        Name = "NewUser"
        Password = "P@ssw0rd!"
        FullName = "New User"
        Description = "Automatically created user"
        PasswordChangeable = $true
        PasswordExpires = $false
    }
    Write-Output "User account 'NewUser' created."
}
Creates a new user account with specified properties.

docs.title: Best Practices for WMI/CIM Automation
docs.text:
1. Prefer CIM over WMI: CIM is more efficient, supports remote management, and aligns with modern standards.
  2. Use -ErrorAction for robustness: Handle errors gracefully in production scripts.
  3. Optimize queries: Filter results with -Filter to reduce data transfer and processing overhead.
  4. Secure remote access: Use Invoke-CimMethod with proper authentication for cross-system management.
  5. Test permissions: Many CIM operations require elevated privileges (e.g., registry edits, user account creation).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Use Get-CimInstance and Invoke-CimMethod for modern, efficient system management.
  • Combine WMI/CIM with filtering and error handling to build robust monitoring and configuration scripts.
  • Prioritize CIM for remote management and complex inventory tasks.
  • Always validate permissions and test scripts in controlled environments before deploying.
  • Leverage CIM’s structured data model for consistent, scalable automation workflows.

docs.title: Just-In-Time (JIT) Administration
docs.text: Just-In-Time (JIT) administration is a security model that grants temporary, role-specific access to administrators or users, reducing the risk of prolonged elevated privileges. Unlike traditional persistent access models, JIT ensures users only have permissions when needed, aligning with the principle of least privilege. This approach minimizes attack surfaces and mitigates risks from compromised credentials or misconfigurations.

docs.title: Enabling JIT Access
docs.text:
To configure JIT access, organizations typically use tools like Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for cloud environments or on-premises solutions like Windows Admin Center or Microsoft Entra ID. The process involves:

  1. Defining roles and permissions: Identify administrative tasks and map them to specific permissions (e.g., SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege, SeDebugPrivilege).
  2. Assigning access: Use role-based access control (RBAC) to grant temporary access to users or groups.
  3. Configuring approval workflows: Set up approval processes for elevated privileges, ensuring accountability.

Example: Using PowerShell to manage JIT policies (hypothetical cmdlets for illustration): 

# Enable JIT for a specific role (example syntax)  
Set-JitPolicy -Role "DomainAdmins" -Enabled $true -Duration 120 # 2 hours  

# Assign temporary access to a user  
Grant-JitAccess -User "admin@example.com" -Role "DomainAdmins" -Approver "approver@example.com"

Note: Actual cmdlets depend on the tooling used (e.g., Azure CLI, Windows Admin Center, or custom scripts). Always verify with official documentation.

docs.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
docs.text:
RBAC is central to JIT, ensuring users receive only the permissions necessary for their tasks. Key steps include:

  1. Creating roles: Define roles based on job functions (e.g., FileServerAdmin, ExchangeAdmin).
  2. Mapping permissions: Assign specific privileges or permissions (e.g., Read/Write access to file shares, Mailbox management).
  3. User assignment: Link users or groups to roles, specifying access duration and conditions.

Example: Configuring a role in Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC): 1. Open ADUC → Right-click the OU → New → Group. 2. Name the group (e.g., FileServerAdmins) and assign permissions via Group Policy or Access Control Entries (ACEs).

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
JIT sessions are ephemeral and automatically expire after a defined period. Key aspects include:

  • Temporary access: Users gain access only during the session, with no persistent credentials stored.
  • Session timeouts: Configure session durations (e.g., 15 minutes) to limit exposure.
  • Logging and auditing: Track session activity for compliance and forensic analysis.

Example: PowerShell script to monitor active JIT sessions (hypothetical): 

Get-JitSession | Where-Object { $_.Duration -gt 0 } | Format-Table User, Role, StartTime, Duration

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• JIT reduces risks by limiting access to only when needed.
  • RBAC ensures granular control over permissions and roles.
  • Session management enforces time-bound access and logging.
  • Integration with PIM or on-premises tools is critical for implementation.
  • Always validate cmdlets and workflows against your environment’s tooling.

docs.title: Just Enough Administration (JEA)
docs.text: Just Enough Administration (JEA) is a PowerShell security model that enables administrators to create restricted, role-based administrative interfaces. By limiting access to specific cmdlets, modules, and execution policies, JEA ensures users can perform only the tasks required for their role, reducing the risk of accidental or malicious damage. This section demonstrates how to configure JEA, restrict cmdlets, and enforce execution policies for secure automation.

docs.title: Creating a JEA Configuration
docs.text:
To create a JEA configuration, define a role capability file (.psrc), which specifies the allowed cmdlets, modules, and execution policies. Here's a basic example:

# Example role capability file: MyJEAConfig.psrc
@{
    RoleCapabilities = @(
        @{
            Role = "MyJEARole"
            Capabilities = @(
                @{
                    Name = "ProcessManagement"
                    Cmdlets = @("Get-Process", "Stop-Process")
                    Modules = @("Microsoft.PowerShell.Management")
                }
            )
            ExecutionPolicy = "Restricted"
        }
    )
}

Save this as MyJEAConfig.psrc in a secure location. Then, create a JEA endpoint using the New-Item cmdlet:

New-Item -Path "C:\JEA\MyJEAConfig.psrc" -ItemType File -Value @'
@{
    RoleCapabilities = @(
        @{
            Role = "MyJEARole"
            Capabilities = @(
                @{
                    Name = "ProcessManagement"
                    Cmdlets = @("Get-Process", "Stop-Process")
                    Modules = @("Microsoft.PowerShell.Management")
                }
            )
            ExecutionPolicy = "Restricted"
        }
    )
}
'@

docs.title: Restricting Cmdlets and Modules
docs.text:
JEA uses role capabilities to control access. For example, to restrict a user to only Get-Process and Stop-Process, define a capability block in the role capability file:

Capabilities = @(
    @{
        Name = "ProcessManagement"
        Cmdlets = @("Get-Process", "Stop-Process")
        Modules = @("Microsoft.PowerShell.Management")
    }
)

To further restrict modules, explicitly list allowed modules and exclude others. For instance, prevent access to Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility:

Modules = @("Microsoft.PowerShell.Management")

Use the Get-JEAConfiguration cmdlet to verify the configuration:

Get-JEAConfiguration -Path "C:\JEA\MyJEAConfig.psrc"

docs.title: Enforcing Execution Policies
docs.text:
